meta.blurb: Bansir builds chariots, Kobbi plays the lute, and at sunset both of them are broke. So they walk across Babylon to Arkad, who started with nothing and is now the richest man in the city. His answer is simpler than they expect.
meta.bible: Babylon: the great walled city of the story, with its market, its river and its clay tablets. Bansir: a chariot-maker, proud of his skill, always short of silver. Kobbi: his friend, a musician who plays his lute at feasts. Arkad: the richest man in Babylon, once a poor scribe, calm and kind; he tells the story. Algamish: the money-lender who hired young Arkad to copy tablets and taught him to keep one part in ten. Dabasir: a former slave who owed many debts and paid every one; his story is on clay tablets from Nippur. Nippur: a city far from Babylon, where the tablets came from. Mathon: a money-lender who helped Dabasir plan his repayments and spoke about borrowing. Hadan: an invented potter, the lucky man who found a purse of silver and lost it again. Invented, unnamed minor figures: a brickmaker, a friend who traded in jewels, camel traders, a sheep farmer, a smiling stranger and two wise men. Money is silver and gold, pieces of silver, shekels and clay tablets; keep ancient detail simple and do not invent historical facts. The seven cures for a lean purse: keep one part in ten of all you earn; control your spending; make your gold work by lending it wisely; guard it against loss and ask the wise; make your home a good investment; plan an income for later; increase your own ability to earn. The five laws of gold are in the story. Voice: calm, wise and slow, like an elder speaking at the end of the day. This is a story about habits and patience, never a promise of riches and never advice for the reader's own money. Added in the full-length book (invented, kept simple, no historical claims): Arkad has a family and a grown son, and owns the small house he bought with his savings; his first loan went to an unnamed brickmaker, who repaid it with a fair payment on top; Arkad's friend in the jewel trade was honest but ignorant of stones; three wise men of the market square (a grain merchant, a cloth trader and a toolmaker) advise him; two grey-bearded wise men help him refuse a stranger who promises to double silver in a month; a caravan master advises him about camel traders, and he lends to several caravans and never to one alone; an unnamed sheep farmer repays him after the wool is sold; an old porter rests by a wall as the lesson of old age; Arkad gives part of his silver each year to those in need. Dabasir was a slave for many years, and his tablets say he was freed owing money to a baker, a cloth-seller, a landlord and others; he worked loading goods for a trader, set aside the creditors' share first, fell ill for a month in his second year, and paid the last piece to the baker. Mathon's table holds clay tablets, scales and bags of silver; Mathon says borrow only what you can repay. In the end Bansir buys the workshop he rented and trains an apprentice, Kobbi teaches young players, each lends a little to a man who knows his trade, and years later they tell a young man by the wall that the secret is only a habit begun on an ordinary day. Language: coins and pieces of silver, clay tablets pressed with a reed, oil lamps, jars; no ink, no tea, no clocks.
chapters: The Potter Who Found a Purse
A Habit on an Ordinary Day

beats.scene: Two tired men sit against a great brick city wall at sunset
beats.summary: Bansir and Kobbi rest by the wall of Babylon after another long day of work.

beats.scene: Bansir turns his empty leather purse upside down beside the city wall
beats.summary: Bansir shows that his purse is empty, although he makes fine chariots.

beats.scene: Bansir holds up his scarred hands beside a half-built chariot wheel
beats.summary: Bansir lists his years of skill and hard work, and how the silver always runs out.

beats.scene: Kobbi holds his lute and shakes his head beside Bansir at dusk
beats.summary: Kobbi admits that his purse is empty too, although he plays at every feast.

beats.scene: A wealthy host laughs at a feast table while Kobbi plays his lute
beats.summary: Kobbi remembers the last feast, where rich men ate well and he went home with a few coins.

beats.scene: Two friends watch lamps being lit across the city as the light fades
beats.summary: The friends, who grew up in the same streets, wonder why their lives are no better than their fathers' lives.

beats.scene: A rich man rides past in a gold-trimmed chariot while two poor friends watch
beats.summary: A rich man passes in a gold-trimmed chariot, followed by running servants.

beats.scene: Bansir stares after the chariot with his empty purse in his hand
beats.summary: Bansir asks why gold comes easily to some men and not to others who work as hard.

beats.scene: Kobbi smiles and points toward the great house of Arkad across the city
beats.summary: Kobbi remembers Arkad, the richest man in Babylon, who is said to have begun with little.

beats.scene: Two friends clasp hands by the wall as the first stars appear
beats.summary: Bansir overcomes his pride, and the friends agree to ask Arkad in the morning.

beats.scene: Bansir lies awake in a small bare room with moonlight at the window
beats.summary: That night Bansir cannot sleep, and he thinks of how he will ask a rich man for help.

beats.scene: Kobbi sits on his doorstep with his lute silent across his knees
beats.summary: Kobbi tries to play but cannot, because his mind is full of questions for Arkad.

beats.scene: Two men in clean robes meet at a street corner as the sun rises
beats.summary: At dawn the friends meet in their cleanest robes and set out for Arkad's house.

beats.scene: Bakers, water carriers and traders crowd a busy market street at morning
beats.summary: The friends walk through the waking market, past bakers, water carriers and traders shouting prices.

beats.scene: Boats unload sacks of grain and jars of oil at the river quay
beats.summary: At the river they see how much wealth passes through Babylon each morning, and how little of it is theirs.

beats.scene: Two friends walk down a quiet, tree-lined street between large houses
beats.summary: The streets grow quiet and wide as the friends enter the part of the city where wealthy people live.

beats.scene: A servant opens a tall gate onto a garden of palm trees
beats.summary: At Arkad's gate a servant hears their request and leads them into the garden.

beats.scene: Two dusty visitors wait on a stone bench beside a pool and palm trees
beats.summary: While they wait in the garden, Bansir grows nervous and wishes he had not come.

beats.scene: Arkad, a calm grey-haired man, walks across the garden toward two visitors
beats.summary: Arkad greets the visitors kindly and asks what brings them to his house so early.

beats.scene: Arkad listens with his head tilted as Bansir speaks with open hands
beats.summary: Bansir asks why men who work hard so often stay poor, and Arkad smiles as if he knew the question well.

beats.scene: Arkad gestures to cushions in the shade as a servant brings water
beats.summary: Arkad invites the friends to sit and says he will answer their question with the story of his own life.

beats.scene: Young Arkad sits cross-legged, pressing a reed into a wet clay tablet
beats.summary: Arkad tells them he was once a poor scribe who copied words onto clay.

beats.scene: A row of clay tablets dries in the sun beside a scribe's low table
beats.summary: A scribe's day was long: he pressed signs into wet clay, and the tablets were baked and sold.

beats.scene: Young Arkad pays for a feast, laughing, with an empty purse in his hand
beats.summary: Arkad spent every coin he earned on food, small gifts and evenings with friends.

beats.scene: A group of young scribes laugh together in a lane of clay workshops
beats.summary: Arkad's friends in the scribes' lane were as poor as he was, and they thought it was simply their fate.

beats.scene: Algamish, a stern, well-dressed money-lender, stands in a doorway looking at tablets
beats.summary: Algamish, a careful money-lender, needed a scribe to copy a long law and chose young Arkad.

beats.scene: Algamish the money-lender hands a pile of clay tablets to young Arkad
beats.summary: Algamish gives Arkad a pile of tablets to copy and promises to pay a fair price.

beats.scene: Young Arkad copies tablets by a small oil lamp late at night
beats.summary: Arkad works until midnight to copy the law without a single mistake.

beats.scene: Algamish counts silver into young Arkad's hand across a table
beats.summary: Algamish pays Arkad fairly and then asks where all of a scribe's silver goes.

beats.scene: Algamish and young Arkad talk across a table lit by a small oil lamp
beats.summary: Arkad admits that he spends all of it, and Algamish says that a man who does so will stay poor.

beats.scene: Algamish leans back in his chair with the lamp light on his face
beats.summary: Algamish says he has seen many scribes with empty purses and offers to teach Arkad the best thing he knows.

beats.scene: Algamish sets one silver piece apart from a row of ten on a table
beats.summary: Algamish sets one piece apart from a row of ten to show what he means.

beats.scene: Algamish taps the table as he speaks to young Arkad
beats.summary: Algamish tells Arkad to keep one part in ten of everything he earns, and to keep it first.

beats.scene: Young Arkad shakes his head with his hand on his empty belt purse
beats.summary: Arkad objects that he cannot live on nine parts, and Algamish answers that he lives on ten and has nothing.

beats.scene: Algamish holds up one finger while Arkad listens with a worried look
beats.summary: Algamish asks him to try it for one year and judge it only at the end.

beats.scene: Young Arkad frowns at nine silver pieces in his hand
beats.summary: Arkad walks home with nine silver pieces and a single one set aside.

beats.scene: Young Arkad drops a silver piece into a clay jar on a shelf
beats.summary: That evening Arkad drops the first piece into a small clay jar and puts it out of reach.

beats.scene: Young Arkad eats bread and dates alone while friends laugh in the street outside
beats.summary: In the first weeks Arkad eats plainer food, and his friends tease him for missing their evenings.

beats.scene: Arkad buys bread and dates at a market stall, smiling
beats.summary: Arkad finds that nine parts are nearly enough, and his jar grows heavy.

beats.scene: Arkad holds up a small clay jar before Bansir and Kobbi in the courtyard
beats.summary: Arkad shows the friends what a jar can do and names the first cure for a lean purse: keep one part in ten.

beats.scene: Arkad sits down in the courtyard with a fresh clay tablet on his knee
beats.summary: Arkad says that keeping a tenth is not enough on its own, and gives the second cure: control your spending.

beats.scene: Arkad draws a line down a clay tablet as the two friends watch
beats.summary: Arkad draws a line down a tablet, with needs on one side and wants on the other.

beats.scene: A clay tablet with a loaf, a roof and a long list of wishes
beats.summary: Needs are few and clear, Arkad says, but wants grow like weeds in a garden.

beats.scene: Kobbi laughs and counts a few silver pieces in his open hand
beats.summary: Kobbi admits how much he spends on small things, such as sweet cakes, wine for friends and ribbons for his lute.

beats.scene: Arkad hands Kobbi a blank clay tablet and a reed
beats.summary: Arkad suggests writing down every purchase for one month.

beats.scene: Bansir holds a polished bronze fitting and looks at it thoughtfully
beats.summary: Bansir says he is careful, then remembers the bronze fittings he bought only to impress his customers.

beats.scene: Arkad raises one finger beside a sunlit wall in the courtyard
beats.summary: Arkad explains that every want feels like a need at the moment of wanting, and advises waiting one day.

beats.scene: Arkad holds up an old scratched tablet covered in tiny marks
beats.summary: Arkad shows his own first tally and tells how surprised he was to see where his silver had gone.

beats.scene: Arkad draws a line between a loaf and a gold ring on a tablet
beats.summary: Arkad says that he never starved his needs, but he never let his wants run loose.

beats.scene: Bansir rubs his chin and looks at Kobbi in the afternoon light
beats.summary: Bansir says that it is easy to say and hard to do, and Arkad agrees that this is why the cures are habits and not secrets.

beats.scene: Young Arkad carries a heavy clay jar through the street toward Algamish's house
beats.summary: After a full year, Arkad carries his jar to Algamish, who asks whether he followed the plan.

beats.scene: Algamish points to a full clay jar while young Arkad looks down
beats.summary: Algamish asks what Arkad has done with his savings, and Arkad admits that the jar only sits on a shelf.

beats.scene: Algamish holds a silver coin up to the lamp light
beats.summary: Algamish explains that idle silver does no work, and that it should be lent with care.

beats.scene: Young Arkad scratches his head as Algamish listens with a patient face
beats.summary: Arkad asks whom he can trust, and Algamish says to lend only to those who have a clear use and a way to repay.

beats.scene: A brickmaker stands beside a stack of unbaked bricks and an empty kiln
beats.summary: Arkad meets a brickmaker who needs silver for clay and fuel to fill a large order.

beats.scene: Young Arkad and a brickmaker agree on terms, holding a clay tablet between them
beats.summary: They agree on a day for repayment and a fair payment on top, and Arkad lends only part of his jar.

beats.scene: Young Arkad lies awake in the dark, staring at the roof
beats.summary: Arkad waits anxiously and wonders whether he will ever see his silver again.

beats.scene: A brickmaker hands a bag of silver back to Arkad beside a kiln
beats.summary: The brickmaker repays Arkad on the day promised, with a fair payment on top.

beats.scene: Young Arkad counts the returned silver in disbelief at his table
beats.summary: Arkad sees that silver he did not work for has earned more silver, and he lends again.

beats.scene: Arkad raises three fingers as the sun lowers behind a palm tree
beats.summary: Arkad names the third cure, to make your gold multiply, and Kobbi asks what happens if a lender loses it.

beats.scene: Arkad shakes his head slowly and looks at the pool in the garden
beats.summary: Arkad admits that he soon made a proud mistake, and that a friend came to him with a plan to trade in jewels.

beats.scene: A smiling friend talks eagerly to young Arkad beside a bright jewel stall
beats.summary: The friend promises great gains from stones bought cheaply far away.

beats.scene: Young Arkad hands silver to a smiling friend beside a jewel stall
beats.summary: Arkad lends a large part of his savings, although neither man knows anything about stones.

beats.scene: Young Arkad waits at the city gate as a tired traveller returns on foot
beats.summary: Months later the friend comes back with a small bag of stones and a worried face.

beats.scene: A grey-haired stone dealer holds up a coloured stone and shakes his head
beats.summary: A dealer looks at the stones and says they are worth almost nothing.

beats.scene: Young Arkad sits alone with his empty purse and a bag of worthless stones
beats.summary: The silver is gone, and Arkad is too ashamed to tell anyone.

beats.scene: Young Arkad stands at Algamish's door with his head down
beats.summary: At last Arkad goes to Algamish and tells him everything.

beats.scene: Algamish pours two cups of water at a table in lamplight
beats.summary: Algamish does not scold him, but tells him that he has now paid for a lesson.

beats.scene: Young Arkad listens carefully to two wise men seated in a market square
beats.summary: Arkad begins to ask those who understand each trade before he lends.

beats.scene: Bansir nods in the garden as Arkad raises four fingers
beats.summary: Arkad names the fourth cure: guard your gold against loss.

beats.scene: Arkad points up at the roof and walls of his home
beats.summary: Arkad names the fifth cure: make a home of your own a good investment.

beats.scene: A young man pays silver to a landlord at a rented door
beats.summary: Young Arkad rented rooms for years, paying a landlord every season and keeping nothing for it.

beats.scene: Algamish leans over a table tapping a clay tablet about houses
beats.summary: Algamish tells Arkad that a man who owns his home keeps his silver in his own family.

beats.scene: Young Arkad stands in front of a small brick house with a courtyard
beats.summary: Arkad buys a small house with part of his savings and repays the rest in small parts.

beats.scene: Arkad's family gathers in a warm courtyard in the evening
beats.summary: Arkad's home becomes a place of comfort, where his family lives without fear of a landlord.

beats.scene: Bansir looks around at a rented workshop with an old chariot in it
beats.summary: Bansir thinks about the workshop that he rents and the silver that goes to its owner.

beats.scene: Arkad gestures toward an old porter resting in the shade of a wall
beats.summary: Arkad names the sixth cure: plan an income for old age and for the family.

beats.scene: An old porter sits against a wall with a heavy basket he cannot lift
beats.summary: The porter once carried heavy loads for merchants, but now his back is bent and his basket is too heavy.

beats.scene: Arkad speaks quietly to two friends in the afternoon light
beats.summary: Arkad says that silver should be put to work now so that it can earn when a man cannot.

beats.scene: Kobbi rubs his fingers and gazes at his lute while Bansir sits quietly
beats.summary: Kobbi realises that a musician's fingers grow stiff with age, and the friends sit together in silence.

beats.scene: Arkad raises seven fingers and smiles at the two friends
beats.summary: Arkad names the seventh cure: increase your own ability to earn.

beats.scene: Bansir shapes the air with his hands as if turning a chariot wheel
beats.summary: Arkad asks Bansir whether he knows his craft as well as any man in Babylon.

beats.scene: Arkad speaks warmly to Bansir with a hand on the garden bench
beats.summary: Arkad says that a man who wishes to learn grows, while a man who stops learning stays small.

beats.scene: Young Arkad copies tablets quickly, with a neat stack beside him
beats.summary: As a young scribe, Arkad learned to copy faster and with fewer mistakes.

beats.scene: Young Arkad reads a long clay tablet at a table while Algamish watches
beats.summary: Arkad learned to read the laws and trade tablets as well as copy them, and Algamish paid him more.

beats.scene: Kobbi strums an imaginary lute and looks up at the sky
beats.summary: Kobbi wonders about learning new songs from other lands and teaching young players.

beats.scene: Bansir sketches a wheel in the dust with a stick
beats.summary: Bansir imagines lighter wheels, stronger axles and an apprentice to share the work.

beats.scene: A servant sets bread, figs and water before three men in a shaded courtyard
beats.summary: Over a simple meal, the three men talk about what they could learn and make.

beats.scene: Arkad breaks a flat loaf of bread with both hands
beats.summary: Arkad reminds them that none of the seven cures works in a day, but each works a little every day.

beats.scene: Arkad looks at a clay tablet in the golden afternoon light
beats.summary: Bansir asks whether there is more to learn, and Arkad says there are laws as well as cures.

beats.scene: Arkad carries a clay tablet to the courtyard table and sets it down
beats.summary: Arkad brings out a tablet and explains that he wrote the five laws of gold long ago for his own son.

beats.scene: Arkad raises one finger beside a clay tablet in the golden afternoon light
beats.summary: The first law of gold: it comes gladly to the one who keeps at least a tenth of what he earns.

beats.scene: A small jar and a larger jar stand side by side on a shelf
beats.summary: A tenth of even a poor man's pay becomes a heavy jar in time.

beats.scene: Arkad weighs a small bag of silver in his open palm
beats.summary: The second law: gold works hard and gladly for a wise owner who finds good work for it.

beats.scene: A bag of silver rests on a table beside a sleeping man's hand
beats.summary: Arkad reminds them that his silver worked while he slept, and never took a day of rest.

beats.scene: Arkad points to a clay tablet while Kobbi and Bansir lean in
beats.summary: The third law: gold stays with the careful owner who asks the advice of the wise.

beats.scene: Three men sit in the market square as a wise man speaks
beats.summary: Advice cost Arkad only a question, and it saved him many pieces of silver.

beats.scene: Arkad holds up a glittering stone and shakes his head
beats.summary: The fourth law: gold slips away when it is put into things the owner does not understand.

beats.scene: Arkad raises a finger as servants light oil lamps in the courtyard
beats.summary: The fifth law: gold flees from those who demand impossible gains or follow tricksters.

beats.scene: Arkad lays down the tablet while Kobbi leans forward with a question
beats.summary: Arkad says the laws are as short as a breath but take a lifetime to keep, and Kobbi asks about luck.

beats.scene: Kobbi leans forward with a puzzled face while Arkad pours water
beats.summary: Kobbi asks about luck, since some men seem to find silver without any effort.

beats.scene: A potter shapes a jar on his wheel in a lane by the river
beats.summary: Arkad tells of Hadan the potter, an honest craftsman who made good jars but stayed poor.

beats.scene: A potter bends to pick up a heavy purse lying on a dusty road
beats.summary: One morning, on the road to market, Hadan finds a heavy purse of silver.

beats.scene: Hadan looks around a dusty road with an open purse in his hands
beats.summary: Hadan asks everyone nearby, but nobody comes forward to claim the purse.

beats.scene: Hadan wears a fine new robe and laughs at a crowded table
beats.summary: Hadan buys a fine robe, gives a feast for his friends and treats himself to a donkey he does not need.

beats.scene: Hadan sits at his potter's wheel with an empty purse beside him
beats.summary: Hadan stops making jars, because he thinks he will never have to work again.

beats.scene: Dry clay cracks on a dusty wheel in an empty workshop
beats.summary: Season after season, the silver goes down, and the clay in his workshop dries and cracks.

beats.scene: Hadan stands at his door looking at a neighbour's busy stall
beats.summary: Hadan's customers go to other potters, and when he wishes to work again, they do not return.

beats.scene: Hadan counts the last coins from the purse at an empty table
beats.summary: At the end of the season, the purse is empty, and Hadan is poorer in habits than he was before.

beats.scene: Arkad lifts a hand toward Kobbi and Bansir in the garden
beats.summary: Arkad tells them that luck gave Hadan silver but no habit to keep it, and that a real habit would have kept the purse.

beats.scene: Arkad lifts baked clay tablets from a wooden chest in lamplight
beats.summary: Arkad answers that luck gives nothing that lasts, and he shows the friends tablets from Nippur.

beats.scene: A bundle of old baked clay tablets lies open on a cloth in lamplight
beats.summary: The tablets were written in Nippur, far from Babylon, by a former slave named Dabasir, and Arkad tells his story.

beats.scene: A thin man carries heavy water jars up a long stone stair
beats.summary: Dabasir spent many years in service as a slave, working hard for others and owning nothing.

beats.scene: A thin man stands in a street with his arms open wide
beats.summary: At last Dabasir was free, but freedom brought a new problem.

beats.scene: A thin former slave stares at a row of clay debt tablets
beats.summary: Dabasir counted his debts and found that he owed money to many people.

beats.scene: Dabasir hurries down a narrow alley with his head down to avoid a baker
beats.summary: Ashamed, Dabasir avoided the streets where his creditors lived and slept badly with worry.

beats.scene: A friend whispers advice to Dabasir at a market stall
beats.summary: A friend tells Dabasir about Mathon, a money-lender known to be fair with those in debt.

beats.scene: Dabasir stands nervously before Mathon, who sits at a table of clay tablets
beats.summary: Dabasir finds Mathon's house and stands before him, unable to speak at first.

beats.scene: Mathon listens with folded hands as Dabasir pours out his story
beats.summary: Dabasir confesses everything, and Mathon says that most men hide from their debts.

beats.scene: Mathon hands Dabasir a blank clay tablet and a reed
beats.summary: Mathon tells Dabasir to write down every debt, with each name and sum, and to return the next day.

beats.scene: Dabasir writes names on a clay tablet by a small lamp late at night
beats.summary: Dabasir writes through the night, listing every name and sum, and the total frightens him.

beats.scene: Mathon reads Dabasir's tablet at his desk in the morning light
beats.summary: Mathon reads the tablet and says that a man who knows his debts has already begun to deal with them.

beats.scene: Mathon asks Dabasir a question across a table of clay tablets
beats.summary: Mathon asks what Dabasir can earn, and Dabasir names the small wage he can find.

beats.scene: Mathon draws a plan with a reed on a fresh clay tablet
beats.summary: Mathon says that Dabasir should live on part of his earnings and share the rest fairly among his creditors.

beats.scene: Dabasir sets small piles of silver beside a row of clay tablets
beats.summary: Mathon shows how each creditor receives a share in proportion to what he is owed.

beats.scene: Mathon points toward the door while Dabasir clutches the tablet
beats.summary: Mathon tells Dabasir to visit every creditor himself and show them the plan.

beats.scene: Dabasir stands at a baker's counter with his tablet held in both hands
beats.summary: At the baker's door, Dabasir's heart pounds, but he explains his plan, and the baker listens.

beats.scene: A stern cloth-seller folds his arms and frowns at Dabasir in a shop
beats.summary: The cloth-seller grumbles but agrees, while another creditor is angry and Dabasir stays calm.

beats.scene: Mathon sets a heavy clay weight on one side of a balance scale
beats.summary: Mathon explains that a man should borrow only what he can repay.

beats.scene: Mathon rests a hand on the scale and speaks to Dabasir at dusk
beats.summary: Mathon warns that loans for pleasure are the heaviest, and sends Dabasir out with a plan.

beats.scene: Dabasir loads sacks onto a camel in the early morning light
beats.summary: Dabasir finds hard work loading goods for a trader and earns his first wages.

beats.scene: Dabasir sets a small pile of silver aside before eating his bread
beats.summary: Each month he sets aside the creditors' share before he spends anything on himself.

beats.scene: A friend waves Dabasir toward a lively feast, but Dabasir turns away
beats.summary: In lean times a friend invites him to a feast, and Dabasir politely refuses.

beats.scene: An angry creditor shouts at Dabasir, who holds up his tablet calmly
beats.summary: One creditor demands everything at once, but Dabasir shows his plan, and Mathon speaks up for him.

beats.scene: A baker crosses a mark off a clay tablet and smiles at Dabasir
beats.summary: Slowly the debts grow smaller, and the baker marks the first one as paid in full.

beats.scene: Dabasir lies ill in a bare room as a neighbour brings him water
beats.summary: Dabasir falls ill and cannot work for a month, and he tells his creditors honestly.

beats.scene: Dabasir leans on a wall as a creditor nods and walks away
beats.summary: The creditors agree to wait, because he has always dealt with them honestly.

beats.scene: Dabasir hands a last piece of silver to a smiling baker
beats.summary: Dabasir is honest with every creditor, keeps his promises and pays the last piece.

beats.scene: Dabasir sleeps peacefully with sunlight on his face and no worries
beats.summary: That night Dabasir owes nothing, and he sleeps more soundly than he has for years.

beats.scene: Kobbi sits quietly with a clay tablet in his lap in the garden
beats.summary: The last tablet says that a man who pays his debts is free, and Kobbi thinks of the baker he owes.

beats.scene: Bansir leans forward in the lamplight with a question on his face
beats.summary: Bansir asks whether Arkad lent to anyone besides the brickmaker, and Arkad says there were many.

beats.scene: Two camel traders bow at Arkad's door with dusty cloaks and a tablet
beats.summary: As Arkad's savings grew, camel traders came to him for silver to buy camels for a caravan.

beats.scene: Arkad listens to a grey-bearded caravan master at a quiet table
beats.summary: Arkad did not say yes at once, but went to a caravan master to ask about the road.

beats.scene: Arkad writes answers on a clay tablet with a reed as a man speaks
beats.summary: He asked how many camels, which road, what cargo and how long, and wrote down every answer.

beats.scene: Arkad shakes hands with two camel traders over a signed clay tablet
beats.summary: Arkad lent only to those who knew their trade, and he took a clear promise.

beats.scene: Camel traders lead a line of camels through the city gate at sunset
beats.summary: The caravan left through the gate at sunset, with camel bells ringing in the dust.

beats.scene: Arkad stands on his roof looking at a wide empty road at night
beats.summary: In the weeks of waiting, news of a sandstorm made Arkad anxious, but he had not lent everything to one caravan.

beats.scene: A camel caravan returns through the gate at dawn with ringing bells

beats.scene: A second caravan arrives late with half-empty baskets on tired camels
beats.summary: Another caravan returns late and has lost part of its goods, and it repays Arkad slowly.

beats.scene: Arkad pours water for his two guests in the courtyard at dusk

beats.scene: A sheep farmer stands at Arkad's gate with his cap in his hands

beats.scene: A flock of sheep crosses green fields beside the river at morning
beats.summary: Arkad visits the farm and sees the flock, and he is glad that the man knows his sheep.

beats.scene: The sheep farmer cradles a newborn lamb in a field at dawn
beats.summary: The farmer tells Arkad that no lamb comes in a day, and that a flock must be fed and waited for.

beats.scene: Brown dry grass and a worried farmer under a hot summer sky
beats.summary: A dry summer thins the grass, and the farmer worries, but Arkad waits patiently.

beats.scene: Farmers shear sheep in a shaded yard while wool piles up in baskets
beats.summary: In autumn the wool is sold, and the farmer repays Arkad with a fair payment on top.

beats.scene: A farmer counts his ewes at sunset beside a stone wall
beats.summary: The farmer did not sell his ewes for quick silver, and Arkad sees that gold grows like a flock when it is kept.

beats.scene: A larger flock moves across a hillside beside a bigger barn
beats.summary: In the second year the flock is larger, and the farmer repays more and soon owns the field.

beats.scene: Arkad speaks with a hand on a garden wall as dusk settles

beats.scene: Kobbi sighs and leans back against a pillar in the evening courtyard
beats.summary: Kobbi says that patience is a hard trade, and Arkad answers that it is learned like any other.

beats.scene: Arkad walks through a busy courtyard while visitors wait with tablets

beats.scene: A smiling stranger in a bright robe holds out a bag at Arkad's door

beats.scene: The stranger bows low and gestures widely in Arkad's doorway
beats.summary: The stranger flatters Arkad as the wisest man in Babylon and speaks with great charm.

beats.scene: The stranger leans close and whispers with a gleaming smile
beats.summary: He promises to double Arkad's silver in a single month, and to take only a small share.

beats.scene: Arkad asks plain questions while the stranger smiles and spreads his hands
beats.summary: Arkad asks what trade, which road and who else has joined, but the stranger has only smiles for answers.

beats.scene: Two grey-bearded wise men sit in Arkad's courtyard beside a clay tablet
beats.summary: Arkad asks two grey-bearded wise men to come and hear the stranger's offer.

beats.scene: Two wise men shake their heads over a tablet while the stranger waits
beats.summary: The wise men study the plan and say that no honest trade doubles silver in a month without great danger.

beats.scene: Arkad holds up a hand as the stranger turns away at the gate
beats.summary: Arkad refuses, and the stranger's smile fades as he leaves the house quickly.

beats.scene: A crowd of worried people stands outside an empty house in the street
beats.summary: Months later, people hear that others gave the stranger their silver and that he vanished with it.

beats.scene: Arkad lifts the old tablet and looks gravely at Bansir in lamplight
beats.summary: Arkad says that when a plan sounds too good to be true, one should ask who gains from it.

beats.scene: Arkad leads two guests through the garden toward a wall at sunset
beats.summary: As the evening deepens, Arkad leads his guests to the garden wall, from which they can see the great wall of the city.

beats.scene: The great wall of Babylon glows in the last light above rooftops
beats.summary: Arkad says that savings are like the city wall: they stand between a family and the wolves of bad luck.

beats.scene: Workers lay bricks in a long row on a half-finished wall
beats.summary: The great wall took many hands and many years, and a purse is built the same way, one brick at a time.

beats.scene: Arkad opens his hands palm up beside a lantern
beats.summary: Arkad says that gold is a tool for a good life and not a prize in itself.

beats.scene: Arkad gives a small bag of silver to a poor woman at the gate
beats.summary: Arkad tells them that he gives part of his silver each year to those in need, and Kobbi is moved.

beats.scene: Arkad rests a hand on Bansir's shoulder at the garden gate at dusk
beats.summary: Arkad says that the habits must be kept for years and not for a day.

beats.scene: Bansir looks at his empty hands under a star-filled sky
beats.summary: Bansir asks how they will know that it is working.

beats.scene: Arkad lifts a clay jar and smiles at the two friends beside him
beats.summary: Arkad answers that at first they will see nothing, but one day a jar will be too heavy to lift with one hand.

beats.scene: Bansir and Kobbi bow to Arkad at the gate with warm thanks
beats.summary: The friends thank Arkad, and he asks them to return in a year and show him their jars.

beats.scene: Bansir and Kobbi walk home together through quiet streets under bright stars
beats.summary: The friends walk home through the quiet city, thinking over everything that they heard.

beats.scene: Bansir and Kobbi stand at a crossroads under a lantern at night
beats.summary: At the crossroads the friends agree to begin the next day, because someday never comes.

beats.scene: Bansir buys a plain clay jar from a potter's stall in morning light
beats.summary: In the morning Bansir buys a plain clay jar and sets it on a high shelf of his workshop.

beats.scene: Kobbi wipes the dust from a cracked old jar in a corner
beats.summary: Kobbi finds an old jar in a corner of his room, cleans it and mends the crack with clay.

beats.scene: Kobbi drops the first silver piece into a clay jar as Bansir watches
beats.summary: That evening Kobbi drops the first piece of silver into his jar while Bansir looks on.

beats.scene: Kobbi plays his lute at a feast while a host counts coins
beats.summary: At a feast, Kobbi sets aside a tenth of his pay before he does anything else.

beats.scene: Kobbi stands before a market stall of bright cloaks, holding his purse
beats.summary: In the first months, Kobbi is tempted by a bright cloak, but he thinks of the jar.

beats.scene: Kobbi turns away from the stall and walks toward the city wall
beats.summary: He walks away from the stall, and the want fades by the time he reaches the wall.

beats.scene: Two friends sit by the city wall each evening, comparing small tablets
beats.summary: The friends meet at the wall each evening and ask each other whether they have set aside their tenth.

beats.scene: Other workers laugh and point at Bansir and Kobbi across a busy street
beats.summary: Some neighbours laugh at them and call them hoarders, but the friends only smile.

beats.scene: Bansir and Kobbi show a heavy clay jar to Arkad in his garden
beats.summary: After one year, the friends carry their jars to Arkad, who lifts one and smiles.

beats.scene: Arkad sets two jars side by side on a stone table and smiles
beats.summary: Arkad tells the friends that now their silver must learn to work, and that they should lend a little to someone who knows his trade.

beats.scene: Bansir talks with a young carpenter beside a bench of new tools
beats.summary: Bansir asks a wise carpenter for advice and then lends a small sum to a young man who needs tools.

beats.scene: Kobbi talks with a maker of reed pipes in a small workshop
beats.summary: Kobbi lends a small sum to a maker of reed pipes, whose work he knows well.

beats.scene: Two friends count a small bag of silver with a fair payment on top
beats.summary: Both loans are repaid with a fair payment on top, and the friends see their silver work for the first time.

beats.scene: Bansir teaches a young apprentice in a larger workshop while Kobbi plays outside
beats.summary: After some years their purses are fatter and their lives are calmer, and Bansir has an apprentice.

beats.scene: Bansir hands silver to a landlord and receives a clay tablet that says paid
beats.summary: Bansir buys the workshop that he used to rent, and the door is truly his own.

beats.scene: Kobbi plays his lute for a group of children in a sunny courtyard
beats.summary: Kobbi plays without the old hurry for coins, and he teaches young players, and his music is better for it.

beats.scene: Arkad, older now, smiles at Bansir and Kobbi in his garden
beats.summary: The friends visit an older Arkad, who tells them that now they are ready to teach.

beats.scene: Two older friends sit by the city wall at sunset with a young man
beats.summary: Years later, the two old friends sit by the wall, and a tired young man with an empty purse sits down beside them.

beats.scene: A young man turns his empty purse upside down as two old friends smile
beats.summary: The young man asks why hard work leaves his purse empty, and the friends answer him kindly, with a habit begun on any ordinary day.

A1A2: Bansir and Kobbi sat by the city wall at the end of the day.
Bansir took out his old purse and turned it over, but nothing fell out.
Bansir said he built a good chariot, but the silver always went away.
Kobbi played music for rich men, but his purse was empty too.
At the last feast, rich men ate well, and Kobbi went home with little.
The two friends had played in these streets as boys, and they were still poor.
A rich man rode by in a gold chariot, and his servants ran behind him.
Bansir asked why gold came so easily to some men and not to him.
Kobbi said they should ask Arkad, the richest man in Babylon.
Bansir put his pride aside, and they agreed to visit Arkad in the morning.
That night Bansir lay awake and thought about what he would say.
Kobbi sat at his door, but he could not play any music.
At dawn the two friends met in their cleanest robes and walked.
The market was busy, and men shouted the prices of bread and wool.
At the river, boats brought grain and oil, but none of it was theirs.
The streets became quiet and wide, and the houses became very large.
A servant opened the tall gate and took them into a garden.
They waited by a pool under the palm trees, and Bansir felt afraid.
Arkad came across the garden and asked what they wanted so early.
Bansir asked why men who work hard so often stay poor.
Arkad asked them to sit down and said he would tell his story.
When Arkad was young, he was a poor man who copied words onto clay.
He pressed a reed into wet clay, and later the tablets were baked.
Arkad spent every coin on food, gifts, and evenings with his friends.
His friends in the lane were poor too, and they thought it was fate.
A money-lender named Algamish needed a man to copy a long law.
Algamish gave Arkad a pile of clay tablets and promised him a fair price.
Arkad worked late into the night and made no mistakes at all.
Algamish paid him well and asked where all his silver went.
Arkad said he spent it all, and Algamish said he would stay poor.
Algamish said he had seen many men with empty purses.
Algamish put one silver piece apart from a row of ten pieces.
He told Arkad to keep one part in ten of everything he earned.
Arkad said he could not live on nine parts, but Algamish disagreed.
Algamish asked him to try it for one year and then decide.
Arkad walked home with nine silver pieces and one set apart.
That night Arkad dropped one piece into a small clay jar.
At first he ate plain food, and his friends laughed at him.
Arkad found that nine parts were nearly enough, and the jar grew heavy.
Arkad held up the jar and said, this is the first cure.
Arkad said the second cure was to control your spending.
He drew a line, with needs on one side and wants on the other.
He said needs are few, but wants grow like weeds in a garden.
Kobbi laughed and said he spent a lot on cakes, wine, and ribbons.
Arkad gave Kobbi a tablet and told him to write down every purchase.
Bansir said he was careful, but then he thought of his bronze fittings.
Arkad said every want feels like a need, so wait for one day.
Arkad showed his old tablet and told how surprised he was.
Arkad never let his needs go hungry, but he did not feed every want.
Bansir said it was easy to say and hard to do.
After a year, Arkad carried his full jar to Algamish.
Algamish asked what he did with the silver, and Arkad said nothing.
Algamish said that silver in a jar does no work, so lend it with care.
Arkad asked whom he could trust, and Algamish gave him one rule.
Arkad met a man who made bricks and needed silver for wood.
They agreed on a day to pay, and Arkad lent only part.
Arkad lay awake and wondered if he would see his silver again.
On the day, the man paid back the silver and a little more.
Arkad saw that silver he did not work for had earned more silver.
Arkad said the third cure was to make your gold grow.
Arkad said that he soon made a mistake, because he was proud.
A friend told him he could win much silver by trading in jewels.
Arkad gave his friend most of his silver, but neither of them knew jewels.
Months later, the friend came home with a small bag of stones.
A dealer looked at the stones and said they were worth almost nothing.
The silver was gone, and Arkad felt too ashamed to tell anyone.
At last, Arkad went to Algamish and told him everything.
Algamish did not shout, and he said Arkad had paid for a lesson.
After that, Arkad asked wise men about each trade before he lent.
Arkad said the fourth cure was to guard your gold from loss.
Arkad pointed to his house and said the fifth cure was to own a home.
For years, Arkad rented rooms and paid a landlord every season.
Algamish said that a man with his own home keeps his silver.
Arkad bought a small house and paid the rest in small parts.
His house became a happy home where his family felt safe.
Bansir thought of his workshop, because he paid rent for it too.
Arkad pointed to an old porter and spoke of the sixth cure.
The old man had carried heavy loads, but now his basket was too heavy.
Arkad said to put your silver to work now, so it can work later.
Kobbi looked at his fingers and thought, one day they will be stiff.
Arkad said the seventh cure was to learn more and earn more.
He asked Bansir if he knew his craft as well as any man.
Arkad said that a man who wants to learn will grow.
As a young man, Arkad learned to copy faster and make fewer mistakes.
He learned to read the laws, and Algamish paid him more.
Kobbi thought about new songs from other lands and teaching young players.
Bansir thought of lighter wheels, stronger axles, and a helper for his shop.
A servant brought bread, figs, and water, and they ate and talked.
Arkad said no cure works in a day, but each works a little every day.
Bansir asked if there was more, and Arkad said there were laws.
Arkad brought out a tablet with five laws that he wrote for his son.
The first law said gold comes gladly to a man who keeps a tenth.
Even a poor man's tenth becomes a heavy jar in time.
The second law said gold works hard for a wise owner.
Arkad said his silver worked while he slept, and it never rested.
The third law said gold stays with careful men who ask the wise.
Advice cost Arkad only a question, and it saved much silver.
The fourth law said gold slips away if you do not understand it.
The fifth law said gold runs from men who want too much too quickly.
The laws are short, said Arkad, but a man needs a lifetime to keep them.
Kobbi asked about luck, because some men find silver without any work.
Arkad told of Hadan, a potter who made good jars but stayed poor.
One morning on the road, Hadan found a heavy purse of silver.
Hadan asked people nearby, but nobody came to take the purse.
Hadan bought a fine robe, gave a feast, and bought a donkey.
Hadan stopped making jars, because he thought he would never need to work.
The silver went down, and the clay in his workshop dried hard.
His customers bought from other potters, and they did not come back.
At the end of the season, the purse was empty.
Arkad said luck gave Hadan silver, but it gave him no good habits.
Arkad said luck gives nothing that lasts, and he opened a box of tablets.
The tablets came from Nippur, and a slave named Dabasir wrote them.
For many years, Dabasir was a slave who worked hard and owned nothing.
At last Dabasir was free, but his freedom brought a new problem.
He counted his debts and found that he owed money to many people.
He felt ashamed, so he stayed away from the streets of his creditors.
A friend told him about Mathon, a money-lender who was fair to men in debt.
Dabasir found Mathon's house and stood before him without a word.
Dabasir told Mathon everything, and Mathon said most men hide from debts.
Mathon gave him a clay tablet and said, write down every debt.
Dabasir wrote all night, and the total of his debts frightened him.
Mathon read the tablet and said that Dabasir had already made a start.
Mathon asked what he could earn, and Dabasir named a small wage.
Mathon said, live on part of it and share the rest.
Each person he owed would receive a share, by the size of the debt.
Mathon told Dabasir to visit each person himself and show the plan.
At the baker's door, his heart beat fast, but the baker listened.
The cloth-seller was unhappy, but he agreed, and one man was angry.
Mathon said a man should borrow only what he can pay back.
Mathon said loans for pleasure are the heaviest, and sent him away.
Dabasir found hard work loading goods for a trader, and he earned wages.
Each month he set aside the share for his creditors before anything else.
A friend asked him to a feast, but Dabasir politely said no.
One man wanted all his money at once, but Mathon spoke for Dabasir.
Slowly his debts grew smaller, and the baker smiled at the first one paid.
Dabasir became ill and could not work for a month.
The creditors agreed to wait, because he had always been honest with them.
At last Dabasir gave the baker the final piece of silver.
That night he owed nothing, and he slept better than he had for years.
The last tablet said that a man who pays his debts is free.
Bansir asked if Arkad lent to anyone else, and Arkad said yes.
As Arkad grew richer, camel traders asked him for silver to buy camels.
Arkad did not say yes at once, but asked a caravan master about the road.
He asked how many camels, which road, and how long, and wrote it all down.
Arkad lent only to men who knew their trade, and he asked for a promise.
The caravan left through the gate at sunset, and the camel bells rang.
Arkad worried about a storm, but he had lent to more than one.
The first caravan came back safely, and the traders paid Arkad a little extra.
Another caravan came late with some goods lost, and it paid Arkad slowly.
Arkad said to lend in many places, and to lend to those who know their trade.
A sheep farmer came to Arkad and asked for silver to buy more sheep.
His plan was lambs in spring, wool in summer, and repayment after.
Arkad visited his farm and was glad that the man knew his sheep.
The farmer said no lamb comes in a day, and a flock must be fed.
The summer was dry, and the grass was thin, but Arkad waited.
In autumn, the wool was sold, and the farmer paid Arkad back.
The farmer did not sell his sheep for quick silver, so the flock grew.
The next year, the flock was larger, and the farmer soon owned his field.
Arkad said many men want a harvest in a week and plant nothing.
Kobbi said patience is hard, and Arkad said it can be learned.
Years later, Arkad's savings had grown, and more people came to his door.
One morning, a stranger in a bright robe came with a wonderful plan.
The stranger said Arkad was a very wise man, and he smiled.
He promised to double Arkad's silver in one month for a small share.
Arkad asked what trade and what road, but the stranger only smiled.
Arkad asked two grey-bearded wise men to come and hear the offer.
The wise men said no honest trade can double silver in a month.
Arkad said no, and the stranger left the house quickly.
Months later, people heard that he took silver from others and vanished.
Arkad said that if a plan sounds too good, ask who gains.
As evening came, Arkad took them to the garden wall.
He said savings are like a city wall that keeps a family safe.
The great wall took many years, and a purse grows the same way.
Arkad said that gold is a tool for a good life, not a prize.
He told them that he gave some silver each year to the poor.
Arkad put a hand on Bansir's shoulder and said, keep the habits for years.
Bansir asked how they would know that the plan was working.
Arkad said, first you will see nothing, but one day the jar will be heavy.
The friends thanked Arkad, and he asked them to return in one year.
The friends walked home through the quiet city under bright stars.
At the crossroads, the friends agreed to begin tomorrow, not someday.
In the morning, Bansir bought a plain clay jar for his workshop.
Kobbi found an old jar, cleaned it, and fixed the crack.
That evening, Kobbi dropped the first silver piece into his jar.
At a feast, Kobbi set aside a tenth of his pay first.
In the first months, Kobbi wanted a bright cloak, but he thought of the jar.
He walked away from the stall, and the want faded before he reached the wall.
Each evening, the friends asked each other if they had saved their tenth.
Some neighbours laughed at them, but the friends only smiled.
After a year, the friends carried their jars to Arkad.
Arkad said their silver must now learn to work, so lend a little.
Bansir asked a wise carpenter first, and then lent to a young man.
Kobbi lent a small sum to a man who made reed pipes.
Both loans came back with a little extra, and the friends smiled.
After some years, their purses were fuller, and Bansir had an apprentice.
Bansir bought the workshop that he once rented, and the door was his own.
Kobbi played without hurry, and he taught young players, and his music was better.
The friends visited Arkad, who said that now they could teach others.
Years later, two old friends sat by the wall, and a tired young man joined them.
The old friends said, begin a habit on any ordinary day.
B1B2: Bansir and Kobbi, two old friends, sat against the great wall of Babylon as the evening sun went down. Both of them were tired and dusty after a long day of work.
Bansir took out his old leather purse and turned it upside down, but nothing fell out. “I make good chariots,” he said, “yet I have never had enough silver.”
Bansir held up his hands, which were scarred by years of wood and bronze. “I have worked hard since I was a boy,” he said, “and still the silver runs away from me.”
Kobbi sighed and rested his lute on his knee, for he knew the same story well. “I play at every feast in the city,” he said, “but the coins slip through my fingers like water.”
At the last feast, rich men had eaten and laughed for hours while Kobbi played for them. When the music ended, he had walked home with only a few coins in his bag.
Across the city, the evening lamps were being lit one by one. The two friends had grown up in the same streets, and they could not see why their lives were no better than their fathers' lives.

A rich merchant rolled past them in a chariot trimmed with gold, and his servants hurried along behind him. Bansir watched the wheels turn, because he knew exactly how much such a chariot cost to build.
Bansir turned his empty purse over once more and stared at the dust. “Why does gold come so easily to some men,” he asked, “and so hard to the rest of us?”
Kobbi stopped and thought, and then he smiled for the first time that day. Everyone said that Arkad was the richest man in Babylon, and some people said he had begun with very little.
Bansir hesitated, afraid that a rich man would laugh at two poor workers. In the end, however, his wish to understand was stronger than his pride, and the friends shook hands.
That night Bansir lay awake in his small room while the moon crossed the window. He practised what he would say to a rich man, and every sentence sounded worse than the last.
Kobbi sat on his doorstep with his lute across his knees, but his fingers would not move. For once in his life, he had more questions than songs.
At dawn the two friends met at the corner of their street, each wearing his cleanest robe. They did not say much, but they set out together towards the house of Arkad.
The market was already alive with bakers, water carriers and traders who shouted the price of dates and wool. The friends pushed through the crowd, and for once nobody tried to sell them anything.

Near the river, boats were unloading sacks of grain and heavy jars of oil onto the stone quay. Bansir saw how much wealth passed through the city each morning, and how little of it ever reached his own hands.

After a while the noise dropped away, and the streets grew wide and quiet and lined with trees. Here the houses stood behind high walls, and the friends felt their old sandals grow heavier with every step.
Kobbi knocked at a tall wooden gate, and a servant looked them over before he spoke. When he heard that two workers wished to ask Arkad a question, he nodded and led them into a garden of palm trees.
They sat on a stone bench beside a pool while the servant went to find his master. Bansir looked at his dusty sandals and wished, for a moment, that he had stayed at home.
Arkad came across the garden slowly, a calm man with grey hair and kind, thoughtful eyes. He did not seem surprised to see two strangers in his house, and he asked what had brought them so early.
Bansir told him about their empty purses and the chariot by the wall, then asked why men who work hard stay poor. Arkad smiled at the question, as if he knew it well.
Arkad asked a servant to bring cushions, water and shade, and the two friends sat down in the garden. “I cannot answer your question in one sentence,” he said, “but I can tell you my own story.”
Many years ago, Arkad said, he had been a poor scribe who copied words onto clay for anyone who paid. He sat cross-legged all day with a reed in his hand, pressing neat signs into wet clay.
A scribe's day was long, and his work was slow and careful. The tablets had to dry in the sun or be baked hard, and he was paid a small amount for each one.
Arkad had never lacked work, but he had never kept the silver he earned. He spent it on food, on small gifts, and on evenings out with his friends, and each night his purse was empty again.

The other young scribes in his lane lived in the same way, and they laughed about their empty purses together. Arkad believed, like them, that poverty was simply the fate of men who worked with their hands.
One day a money-lender named Algamish, a stern and careful man, needed someone to copy a long law. He asked around the lane for the best scribe, and the other men pointed at Arkad.
Algamish handed him a pile of clay tablets and said that the copy must be perfect. He promised a fair price, and Arkad, who was not used to being trusted, felt proud and a little afraid.
That night Arkad lit a small oil lamp and worked on the law for many hours. He was tired by midnight, but he did not make a single mistake, because he wanted to prove himself.

When Arkad brought the finished tablets, Algamish read them carefully and paid him exactly what he had promised. Then he looked up and asked a question that Arkad never forgot: where does all of a scribe's silver go?
Arkad felt his face grow warm, but he did not lie. He admitted that he spent every piece of it, and Algamish nodded slowly and said that a man who does so will always stay poor.
Algamish leaned back in his chair and looked at the young scribe for a long time. He said that he had seen many men with empty purses, and that he would teach Arkad the best thing he knew.
He pulled ten pieces of silver from his bag and set them in a row on the table. Then he slid one piece a little apart from the others, and he asked Arkad what he saw.

Algamish tapped the table with one finger, and he spoke slowly so that every word would be remembered. “Keep one part in every ten that you earn,” he said, “and keep it before you pay for anything else.”
Arkad shook his head, for he could not see how a man who lived on ten parts could live on nine. Algamish answered that he already lived on ten, and that the result was an empty purse.
Then Algamish raised one finger and made a simple request. Arkad should try the plan for one year, and only at the end of it should he decide whether it was foolish.
Arkad frowned all the way home, holding nine silver pieces in his hand and thinking about the tenth. He was not at all sure that he could do what the money-lender had asked.
That evening, however, he found a small clay jar and dropped the first piece of silver into it. He set the jar on a high shelf, where he would see it every day but could not easily reach it.
In the first weeks he ate plain bread and dates, and he said no to many pleasant evenings. His friends teased him in the lane and asked where the cheerful Arkad had gone.
Little by little, Arkad discovered that nine parts were nearly enough. Each week another piece went into the jar, and one day he lifted it and noticed that it had become heavy.

In the garden, Arkad held up the same small jar, now old and chipped, and gave Bansir and Kobbi a quiet look. “This,” he said, “is the first cure for a lean purse: keep one part in ten of everything you earn.”
Arkad sat down with a fresh clay tablet on his knee and told his visitors that saving was only the beginning. The second cure, he said, is to control your spending.
With his reed, Arkad drew a line down the middle of the tablet. On the left he would write what a man needs, and on the right he would write what a man only wants.

Needs are few and easy to name, Arkad said: bread, a roof, a robe and the tools of one's work. Wants, however, are like weeds in a garden, because they come up everywhere and grow faster than anything useful.
Kobbi laughed and counted a few silver pieces in his open hand, and then his smile faded. He admitted that he spent too much on sweet cakes, on wine for friends and on ribbons for his lute.

Arkad spoke quietly to his guests, because he did not wish to be heard by the old man. Silver must be put to work now, he said, so that it will be earning when a man's strength is gone.
Kobbi rubbed his fingers and looked down at his lute. He had never thought about the day when his hands would grow stiff, and the two friends sat together in thoughtful silence.
Arkad raised seven fingers and smiled at the two friends. “The seventh cure,” he said, “is to increase your own ability to earn, for skilled hands are the best purse.”
Arkad turned to Bansir and asked whether he knew his craft as well as any man in Babylon. Bansir thought for a moment and was surprised to find that he could not say yes.

A man who wishes to learn will grow, Arkad said, and a man who stops learning will always stay small. He added that people who know their work well are paid for their knowledge and not only for their effort.
When Arkad was a young scribe, he had worked to copy faster and with fewer mistakes. Within a year, the lane had begun to say that Arkad's tablets were the cleanest in the city.
He had also learned to read the laws and the trade records that he copied, instead of only pressing them into clay. Algamish noticed, and he began to pay Arkad more than the other scribes.
Kobbi stared up at the sky and strummed an imaginary lute with his fingers. He had never learned the songs of other lands, and he wondered whether young players would pay to learn from him.
Bansir drew a wheel in the dust with a stick and then drew a lighter one beside it. He imagined a stronger axle, and he imagined an apprentice to share the work and learn the craft.
A servant brought bread, figs and cool water on a tray and set it on a low table in the shade. The three men ate slowly and talked about what each of them might learn and make.
Arkad broke a flat loaf in half and handed one piece to each guest. None of the seven cures works in a day, he said, but each one works a little every day if it is kept.
Bansir looked at the empty tablet in front of him and asked whether there was anything more to learn. Arkad answered that the cures tell a man what to do, but that five laws of gold explain why.

Arkad went into the house and came back with a clay tablet, which he set down on the courtyard table. Long ago, he said, he had written five laws of gold for his own son, who was leaving home to find his own fortune.

Arkad raised one finger beside the tablet and spoke slowly, so that nobody could miss a word. “The first law is that gold comes gladly to the man who keeps at least a tenth of what he earns,” he said.
A tenth of even a poor man's pay becomes a heavy jar in time, he told them. The jar does not grow because the man is clever, but because he keeps on adding to it, week after week.
Arkad weighed a small bag of silver in his open palm and smiled. “The second law is that gold works hard and gladly for the wise owner who finds good work for it,” he said.
Arkad reminded them that his silver had earned more silver while he slept, and while he ate, and while he walked in the market. Gold, unlike a man, never asks for a day of rest.
Kobbi and Bansir leaned closer as Arkad pointed to the next line of the tablet. “The third law is that gold stays with the careful owner who asks the advice of the wise,” he said.
Arkad said that the advice of the wise had cost him only a question, and that a question had saved him many pieces of silver. He thought it was the cheapest bargain he had ever made.
Arkad lifted a glittering stone from a bowl and shook his head. “The fourth law is that gold slips away when it is put into things that the owner does not understand,” he said.

As the shadows grew longer, servants came and lit the oil lamps in the courtyard. “The fifth law,” said Arkad, “is that gold flees from those who demand impossible gains or who follow tricksters and schemers.”
Arkad laid the tablet down gently, and he said that the laws were as short as a breath. A man needs a whole lifetime to keep them, he added, and Kobbi leaned forward with a new question about luck.
Kobbi leaned forward with a puzzled look while Arkad poured water for his guests, and he asked about luck. It seemed to him that some men found silver without any effort at all.
Arkad smiled and said that he would tell them about Hadan the potter. Hadan lived in a lane beside the river, and he made fine jars, but he had never been able to keep any silver for long.

One morning, Hadan was pulling his cart of jars along the road to market when he saw something lying in the dust. It was a heavy purse, and when he opened it, he found more silver than he could earn in a year.
Hadan looked up and down the road, but there was nobody to be seen. He asked every traveller he met whether a purse had been lost, and nobody came forward to claim it.
At last Hadan decided that the silver was his, and he made up for all the years of being poor. He bought a fine robe, gave a great feast for his friends and bought a donkey that he did not need.
Soon he stopped making jars, because he believed that he would never have to work again. His wheel stood still, and he sat beside it with an empty cup and a full purse, feeling very rich.
Season after season, the silver in the purse grew less, and the clay in his workshop dried and cracked. Hadan told himself that he would begin again tomorrow, but tomorrow never seemed to come.
Meanwhile his old customers began to buy their jars from other potters in the lane. When Hadan finally wished to work again, he found that they had forgotten him.
By the end of the year, the purse was empty and Hadan was poorer than ever. He sat down at his table and counted the last coins, and he could not understand where all that luck had gone.
Arkad lifted a hand toward his guests in the garden. “Luck gave Hadan silver,” he said, “but it did not give him a habit to keep it, and a habit would have kept the purse.”
Arkad said that luck gives nothing that lasts, and he went to fetch a wooden chest. Inside, wrapped in cloth, lay a bundle of baked clay tablets, and he laid them out carefully in the lamplight.
These tablets had come from Nippur, a city far from Babylon, and a former slave named Dabasir had written them. Arkad said that he would tell the story as the tablets told it.
Dabasir had spent many years in service as a slave, carrying water and building walls for other men. He worked hard all day, but he owned nothing at all, not even his own name for a while.
At last the day came when Dabasir was free, and he walked out into the street with his arms open. For a short time he was happy, but then he remembered something that freedom could not wash away.

He sat down and counted his debts on a row of clay tablets, and the sums were larger than he had feared. Some came from the foolish days before he was sold, and some he had taken on since, and he owed money to many people.

Dabasir was so ashamed that he began to avoid the streets where his creditors lived. He hurried down alleys with his head bowed, and at night he lay awake, hearing every footstep as a knock at the door.
After some weeks, a friend whispered to him in the market that there was a money-lender named Mathon. Mathon was known to be fair, the friend said, even to men who owed a great deal.
Dabasir found Mathon's house at last and stood before a table crowded with clay tablets. His mouth was dry, and for a long time he could not say a word.

Mathon sat with his hands folded and waited until Dabasir found his voice, and then Dabasir told him everything. Mathon said that most men hide from their debts, and that few were brave enough to come.
Mathon gave him a blank tablet and a reed, and he gave him a simple task. Dabasir should write down every debt, with the name of every creditor and every sum, and come back the next day.
Dabasir sat up all night by a small lamp, writing every name and every sum on the clay. When he added up the total at dawn, the number was so large that his hand shook.
The next morning, Mathon read the tablet slowly and then looked up with a kind expression. He said that a man who knows exactly what he owes has already begun to deal with it.
Mathon asked how much silver Dabasir could earn in a month if he worked hard. Dabasir named a small wage, which was all that a freed slave could hope to find, and Mathon nodded.
With a reed, Mathon drew a plan on a fresh tablet. Dabasir would live on part of his earnings, he said, and the rest would be shared fairly among the people he owed.

Mathon laid out small piles of silver beside a row of tablets and showed how the sharing would work. Each creditor would receive a part in proportion to what he was owed, so that nobody was treated better than another.
Then Mathon pointed to the door and told Dabasir that he must visit every creditor himself. He should show each one the tablet and explain the plan honestly, face to face.

At the baker's door, Dabasir's heart pounded, and he held his tablet in both hands like a shield. The baker listened to the whole plan, and he said that he would rather have a little each month than nothing at all.
The cloth-seller folded his arms and grumbled loudly, but in the end he agreed. Another creditor was angry and raised his voice, yet Dabasir stayed calm and showed him the tablet again.
On Dabasir's return, Mathon set a heavy clay weight on one side of a balance scale. A man should borrow only what he can repay, he said, and he should think about the weight before he takes it up.
