Each month, before he spent a single piece on himself, Dabasir set aside the creditors' share. He did not wait to see what was left over, because he knew that nothing would ever be left over.
There were lean times, and in one of them a friend invited him to a lively feast with music and roast meat. Dabasir thanked him warmly and refused, and he went home to his bread and his tablet.
One creditor lost his patience and demanded all his silver at once. Dabasir held up the tablet calmly and showed the plan, and Mathon himself came to speak up for him.
Slowly, the debts began to grow smaller, and the marks on the tablets showed it. The baker, with a broad smile, drew a line through the first debt and wrote the word paid.
In the second year, Dabasir fell ill and could not work for a month. He did not hide, but went to every creditor and told them honestly what had happened.
The creditors agreed to wait, because Dabasir had always dealt with them fairly and kept every promise. When he recovered, he worked harder than ever, and the share he set aside was never late.
At last the day came when Dabasir walked to the baker's shop with the final piece of silver. The baker took it, laughed aloud and clasped his hand as though they had been friends for years.
That night, Dabasir owed nothing to anyone, and he slept more soundly than he had slept in years. In the morning, he walked down the street with his head high and looked every man in the eye.
The last tablet said that a man who pays his debts is truly free, and that he should then keep a tenth. Kobbi thought of the baker he owed and found that he was blushing.

Bansir leaned forward in the lamplight and asked whether Arkad had lent to anyone besides the brickmaker. Arkad laughed softly and said that there had been many, because as his savings grew, people came to him more and more.
One year, two camel traders in dusty cloaks came to his door with a tablet in their hands. They needed silver to buy camels for a caravan, and they promised to repay him when they returned.
Arkad did not say yes at once, but went to a grey-bearded caravan master who knew the desert roads. He asked the old man many questions about camels, prices and trade.
He asked how many camels they needed, which road they would take and how long they would be gone. He wrote down every answer on a clay tablet, so that he could think about it later.
Arkad lent only to those who knew their trade well, and he asked for a clear promise on a tablet. He shook hands with the two traders over the signed clay, and they thanked him with great respect.
The caravan left through the city gate at sunset, and the camel bells rang softly in the dust. Arkad watched until the last animal had disappeared into the fading light.

In the weeks of waiting, a rumour of a desert storm reached the city, and Arkad watched the empty road from his roof. He was anxious, but he knew that he had not lent all of his silver to one caravan.
At last, one early morning, the first caravan came back through the gate with its bells ringing. The traders were tired but happy, and they repaid Arkad in full, with a fair payment on top.
A second caravan arrived many days later with half-empty baskets and tired camels. It had lost some goods and repaid Arkad slowly, but he had spread his silver, so the loss did not hurt him.

Arkad poured water and said that gold lent in many places, to people who know their trade, is guarded by the spread. “One caravan may fail,” he said, “but a wise lender does not let one caravan decide his fortune.”
Another year, a sheep farmer in a woolly hat came to Arkad's gate with his hat in his hands. He asked for silver to buy more ewes, and he spoke simply, like a man who is used to the open air.
He drew his plan in the dust with his crook. Lambs would be born in the spring, wool would be sheared in the summer, and he would repay Arkad when the wool was sold.
Arkad went out to see the farm, and he found a flock of sheep spread over green fields beside the river. He was glad to see that the farmer knew each animal and spoke to it by name.
At dawn, the farmer held a newborn lamb in his arms and told Arkad that no lamb comes in a day. A flock must be fed and watched, he said, and a man must be willing to wait for its seasons.
That summer was dry, and the grass grew thin and brown under the hot sun. The farmer worried, but Arkad did not ask for his silver early, because he had agreed to wait.
In the autumn, the rains came, the sheep were sheared, and the wool was sold at the market. The farmer came to Arkad with a heavy bag and repaid him, with a fair payment on top.
The farmer had not sold his ewes for quick silver, though he had been tempted. Arkad saw that gold grows like a flock when it is kept and fed, and that it fails when it is eaten too soon.
In the second year, the flock was larger, and the farmer repaid Arkad even more. Before long, he owned the field where his sheep had grazed, and he built himself a bigger barn.
Arkad rested a hand on the garden wall as the evening settled around them. Many men want a harvest in a week, he told Bansir, and so they never plant anything at all.
Kobbi sighed and leaned back against a pillar, and he said that patience is a hard trade. Arkad answered that it is learned like any other, one small day at a time.
Years went by, and Arkad's savings had grown so much that the whole city knew his name. More and more people came to his door, and many of them brought plans, requests and tablets full of promises.
One morning, a stranger in a bright robe arrived at the gate with a bag in his hand. He smiled at the servant so warmly that the servant almost let him in without asking his name.
The stranger bowed low and called Arkad the wisest man in all of Babylon. His words were smooth and flattering, and each one seemed to be chosen to please.

Leaning close, he whispered that he knew of a secret trade that could double Arkad's silver in a single month. He would take only a small share for himself, he said, and Arkad could not possibly lose.
Arkad asked a few plain questions: which trade, which road and who else had joined. The stranger spread his hands and smiled, and he answered with long speeches that did not answer anything.
Arkad said that he would think about it, and he sent a servant to fetch two grey-bearded wise men. They came at once and sat down in the courtyard with a clay tablet between them.
The wise men studied the stranger's plan for a long time, and then they shook their heads. No honest trade doubles silver in a month, they said, without great danger to those who lend.
Arkad refused, politely but firmly, and he thanked the stranger for coming. The stranger's smile faded, and he hurried away from the gate with his bag held tightly under his arm.
Months later, news ran through the city that the stranger had taken silver from many people. When they came to look for him, they found only an empty house and a few broken promises.
Arkad lifted the old tablet and looked at Bansir in the lamplight. “When a plan sounds too good to be true,” he said, “it is wise to ask who really gains from it.”
As the evening deepened, Arkad led his guests across the garden to the far wall. From there, the great wall of Babylon stood above the rooftops, glowing in the last light of the sun.

Arkad said that savings are like a city wall, because they stand between a family and the wolves of bad luck. A man does not notice them on a calm day, he said, but he is glad of them on a stormy night.
The great wall had taken many hands and many years to build, Arkad reminded them. A purse is made in the same way, one brick at a time, and no single brick looks important by itself.
He opened his hands, palms up, beside a lantern. Gold is a tool for a good life, he said, and it is never a prize in itself.
Arkad told them that each year he gave part of his silver to those who were in need. Kobbi was moved by this, and he saw that the richest man in Babylon valued his gold less than his friends.
At the garden gate, Arkad rested a hand on Bansir's shoulder. “These habits must be kept for years,” he said, “and not for a day, however bright the day may be.”
Bansir looked at his empty hands under the stars, and he asked how they would know that the plan was working. He was not doubting Arkad, but he was afraid of being disappointed again.
Arkad lifted his old jar and smiled, and he said that at first they would see nothing at all. But one day, he said, the jar would be too heavy to lift with a single hand.
The friends thanked Arkad with all their hearts and bowed at the gate. Arkad said that they should come back in a year and show him their jars, and that he would be glad to see them.
Bansir and Kobbi walked home together through the quiet streets, under a sky full of bright stars. They did not talk much, because both of them were thinking over everything that they had heard.
At the crossroads, under a hanging lantern, the two friends stood still for a moment. They agreed to begin the very next day, because they both knew that someday never comes by itself.
In the morning, Bansir bought a plain clay jar from a potter's stall in the market. He took it back to his workshop and set it on a high shelf, where he would see it every day.
Kobbi had no new jar, but he found an old one in the corner of his room. He wiped away the dust, mended a crack with clay and set it down beside his bed.

That evening, Kobbi held a single silver piece over the mouth of the jar while Bansir looked on. When the coin dropped inside, it made a small sound, and the two friends smiled at each other like boys.

At the next feast, Kobbi played well and was paid as usual, and he counted the coins carefully when he got home. Before he did anything else, he set aside a tenth of them and dropped them into the jar.

In the first months, Kobbi often passed a market stall of bright cloaks with his purse in his hand. One cloak in particular, the colour of the evening sky, pulled at him, and he stood in front of it for a long time.
At last he thought of the jar and turned away from the stall. By the time he reached the city wall, the wish had faded, and he was almost surprised to find that it had gone.

Each evening, the friends met at the wall and asked one another if they had set aside their tenth. It was a small question, but it was easier to keep a promise that someone else was waiting to hear about.

Some neighbours laughed at them and called them hoarders, and a few said they were wasting their lives. Bansir and Kobbi only smiled, because the jars were growing heavier and the laughter was growing lighter.
After one full year, the friends carried their jars through the quiet quarter to Arkad's garden. Arkad lifted one, felt its weight and smiled, as though he had been waiting for them all that time.
Arkad set the two jars side by side on a stone table and smiled. Now, he said, their silver must learn to work, and they should lend a little to someone who knew his trade.

Bansir first asked a wise carpenter what he thought, and the old man said that the young man in question was honest and skilled. Then Bansir lent a small sum so that the young man could buy new tools.
Kobbi lent a small sum to a maker of reed pipes, whose work he had known for many years. He had played the man's pipes at a hundred feasts, and he could hear for himself that they were good.
Both loans were repaid on the day that had been agreed, with a fair payment on top. The two friends counted the silver and smiled, because for the first time they had seen their own savings at work.
After some years, their purses were fatter, and their lives were calmer. Bansir moved into a larger workshop with an apprentice, and he taught the boy as carefully as he had once been taught.

One spring morning, Bansir put his silver on a landlord's table and received a clay tablet that said the workshop was paid for. He walked home slowly, touching the doorframe of his own shop as though it might disappear.

Kobbi played at feasts without the old anxious hurry for the coins, and his music was better for it. He also taught young players on the quiet afternoons, and the children of the lane learned to love the lute.
When Arkad was older, the friends visited him again in the quiet garden, and they told him all that had happened. He listened with great pleasure, and he told them that now they were ready to teach.
Many years later, the two old friends sat by the great wall at sunset, as they did on most evenings. A young man with a tired face and dusty sandals sat down beside them and said nothing.
The young man turned his empty purse over and asked why hard work always left it so light. The old friends smiled and told him that there was no secret, only a habit that begins on any ordinary day.
