Bansir hesitated, for it is a hard thing for a proud man to knock at a rich man's door and admit that his own purse is empty. Yet the question had troubled him for years, and he knew that another year of silence would answer nothing. They clasped hands as the first stars appeared above the wall and agreed to go at first light.

That night Bansir lay awake in his small room while the moon travelled slowly across the window. He rehearsed what he would say to a rich man, and each sentence sounded humbler and more foolish than the one before. Toward midnight he gave up the attempt and simply listened to the city breathing outside his shutters.

Kobbi sat on his doorstep with the lute across his knees, but for once his fingers refused to answer him. He had played at a hundred feasts without a flicker of nerves, yet the thought of facing one quiet old man made his hands unsteady. He realised, with some surprise, that he had more questions in him than songs.

At dawn the two friends met at the corner of their street, each in the cleanest robe he owned, and exchanged a look of nervous determination. Neither of them said much, for there was little left to say that the night had not already said. They set off together toward the quiet quarter where Arkad lived, walking a little faster than usual.

The market was already alive with bakers, water carriers and merchants who shouted the price of dates and wool above the clatter of carts. The friends pushed through the crowd, and for once nobody tried to sell them anything, as though the sellers could smell the emptiness of their purses. Bansir kept his eyes ahead, afraid that if he stopped, he would lose his courage.

Near the river, flat boats were unloading sacks of grain, jars of oil and bundles of cloth onto the stone quay, and porters swarmed over them like ants. Bansir paused to watch, struck by how much wealth passed through Babylon in a single morning. It occurred to him that someone must own every sack and jar, and that none of those someones was himself.

Gradually the noise fell away, and the road widened into streets lined with shade trees, where the houses stood behind tall walls and the air smelled of flowers. Here the only sound was the slap of the friends' worn sandals on the clean stone. Kobbi felt as though the city itself had grown quiet to listen to their errand.

Kobbi knocked at a tall wooden gate, and a servant looked them over from head to foot before he spoke. When he heard that two workers wished to ask the master a question about gold, a faint smile crossed his face, and he stepped aside. He led them through the gate into a garden of palm trees where a fountain murmured to itself in the shade.

They sat on a stone bench beside a pool while the servant went to find his master, and the water threw small bright rings of light across the leaves above. Bansir looked at his dusty sandals and the frayed hem of his robe, and for a moment he wished with all his heart that he had stayed at home. Kobbi, who could sense his friend's doubt without a word, laid a steady hand quietly on his arm.

Arkad came across the garden slowly, a calm man with grey hair and kind, thoughtful eyes that seemed to take in everything at once. He did not appear surprised to find two dusty strangers waiting in his house, and he greeted them as courteously as if they had been merchants of the highest rank. He asked what had brought them to his gate at so early an hour.

Bansir described their empty purses and the gold-trimmed chariot that had rolled past them beside the wall. He put his question plainly, asking why men who labour from sunrise to sunset so often remain poor all their lives. Arkad neither laughed nor frowned, but simply smiled, like a man who has heard a question that he once asked himself.

Arkad asked a servant to bring cushions, cool water and a little shade, and the two friends sank gratefully onto the garden seats. “I cannot answer your question in a single sentence,” he said, “but I can tell you honestly how my own purse came to be full.” His voice was unhurried, like that of a man accustomed to being listened to, and yet it carried no pride.

Many years ago, Arkad said, he had been a poor scribe, copying words onto clay for anyone who could afford the price. He had sat cross-legged from morning until dusk with a reed in his fingers, pressing neat rows of signs into soft, wet tablets. His hands had been stained with clay, and his purse had been lighter than either of his visitors could imagine.

A scribe's day was long and slow, for each tablet had to be written with care and then left to dry in the sun or baked until it was hard. Rows of them lined the benches of the lane like loaves in a bakery, and each one earned only a modest sum. The work demanded patience and a steady hand, and it rewarded neither with anything more than enough for supper.

Arkad had never lacked for work, but he had never kept the silver it brought him. He spent it on food, on small gifts for people he liked, and on long evenings with friends, and by nightfall the purse at his belt was always empty again. He told himself that this was simply what money was for, and he never stopped to ask where the silver had gone.

The other young scribes in his lane lived in much the same way, and they would laugh together over their empty purses as though poverty were a joke that all of them shared. Arkad believed, as they did, that being poor was the natural fate of men who earned their bread with their hands. It never occurred to him that anyone in the world might be making a different choice.

One day a money-lender named Algamish, a stern, careful man known for the cleanliness of his accounts, needed someone to copy a long and complicated law. He asked around the lane for the best scribe available, and one by one the other young men pointed toward Arkad. The choice surprised him, for no one had ever singled him out for anything before.

Algamish placed a heavy pile of clay tablets into his hands and warned him that the copy must be perfect in every line. He promised a fair price for the work, and Arkad, who was not accustomed to being trusted, felt proud and a little frightened at the same moment. He carried the tablets home as carefully as if they had been made of glass.

That night Arkad lit a small oil lamp, set the first tablet in front of him and worked on the law for hour after hour. By midnight his shoulders ached and his eyes burned, but he did not make a single mistake, because for the first time in his life he wanted to prove that he could be relied upon. The lamp guttered low as the city slept, and the clay slowly filled with his careful signs.

When Arkad brought the finished tablets back, Algamish read through them with a sharp eye and paid him exactly the price he had promised. Then the money-lender looked up, set the silver on the table, and asked the question that Arkad would remember for the rest of his life. He wished to know where all of a scribe's silver went, since a man who worked so carefully ought to have something to show for it.

Arkad felt his face grow warm, but he had no wish to lie to a man who had treated him so fairly. He admitted that he spent every piece of silver he earned, and that his purse was empty almost before the clay was dry. Algamish nodded slowly, as if the answer were exactly what he had expected, and told him that a man who lives in that way will always remain poor.

Algamish leaned back in his chair, with the lamplight carving deep lines in his face, and studied the young scribe for a long, silent moment. He said that he had watched many men labour all their lives for nothing, and that he was willing to teach Arkad the best thing he knew. It was an unexpected kindness from a man who was not known for giving things away.

He drew ten pieces of silver from his bag and set them in a neat row on the table. With one finger he slid a single piece away from the rest, and he asked Arkad to say plainly what he saw. Arkad could see nothing but nine coins and a tenth that stood alone, and he waited, puzzled, for the lesson to begin.

Algamish tapped the wooden table with one finger as he spoke, and each word fell as heavily as a coin. “Keep one part in every ten that you earn,” he said, “and keep it before you pay a single bill, buy a single loaf or lend a single coin.” He did not shout, or even smile, for in his own mind he was simply stating a fact.

Arkad shook his head, for he could not see how a man who had never lived on less than ten parts could possibly manage on nine. Algamish replied, without unkindness, that Arkad was already living on all ten parts and that the result was a purse as empty as a cracked bowl. If ten parts had not made him comfortable, he said, then nine could hardly make him worse off.

Then Algamish raised a single finger and made a modest request that was hard to refuse. Arkad should follow the plan for one full year, and only when the year had ended should he judge whether it had been foolish or wise. A man who rejects an idea before he has tried it, the money-lender added, learns nothing from either result.

Arkad frowned the whole way home, with nine silver pieces in his fist and the thought of the tenth pulling at his mind like a stone in his sandal. He was far from certain that he could do what the money-lender had asked, or that he wished to try. Yet he could not forget the calm certainty with which the old man had spoken.

That evening, however, he found a small clay jar in the corner of his room and dropped the first piece of silver into it with a faint, hollow chink. He set the jar on a high shelf, where he would see it every day but could not reach it without effort. It was a small beginning, and he felt a little foolish, but he left the jar where it was.

In the first weeks he ate plain bread and dates and declined many pleasant evenings, and the other scribes teased him mercilessly in the lane. They asked where the cheerful Arkad had gone and whether he had become too grand to drink with his old friends. He bore it with as much humour as he could, though more than once he stood in the doorway of a feast and felt his resolve falter.

Little by little, however, Arkad made a surprising discovery, which was that nine parts were nearly enough for him to live on. Each week another piece went into the jar, and one evening he lifted it from the shelf and noticed, with a thrill of astonishment, that it had become heavy. He had never in his life owned anything that grew simply because he left it alone.

In the garden, Arkad held up the same small jar, now old and chipped at the rim, and gave Bansir and Kobbi a quiet, steady look. “This,” he said, “is the first cure for a lean purse, and it is simpler than you imagined: keep one part in every ten that you earn.” The two friends stared at the humble clay vessel as though it were a king's treasure chest.

Arkad settled himself in the courtyard with a fresh clay tablet across his knee and told his visitors that saving was only the beginning of the matter. A man might put aside a tenth of everything and still waste the rest, he said, and so there was a second cure that must go beside the first. It was the cure of controlling one's spending, and it was the one that most people liked least.

With his reed, Arkad drew a single straight line down the middle of the tablet, dividing the clay into two equal halves. On the left, he explained, he would write the things that a man truly needs, and on the right he would write the things that he merely wants. The friends leaned closer, for they could already guess how unequal the two columns would turn out to be.

Needs are few and easy to name, Arkad said: bread to eat, a roof overhead, a robe against the cold and the tools of one's trade. Wants, on the other hand, are like weeds in a garden, because they spring up everywhere, flourish without care and crowd out everything useful that was planted. A man who does not watch his wants, he added, will soon find that he is tending a jungle instead of a field.

Kobbi laughed and began counting the few silver pieces that lay in his open hand, but his smile faded as he did so. He confessed that he spent far more than he liked to admit on honeyed cakes, on wine for friends who rarely paid him back and on bright ribbons for his lute. Each of these purchases had seemed trifling at the time, yet he now had the uneasy feeling that together they might have made a respectable fortune.

Arkad held out a blank tablet and a clean reed and set Kobbi a simple, practical task. For one whole month he should write down every single thing that he bought, no matter how small or how foolish it seemed. There is nothing like a written list, Arkad said, for turning a vague feeling into a plain and unmistakable fact.

Bansir declared that he was a careful man and suffered from no such weakness. Then he remembered the gleaming bronze fittings that he had bought for a rich man's chariot, not because the wheels required them but because they looked so grand, and he lapsed into an awkward silence. Arkad, who missed nothing, merely smiled and let the thought do its quiet work.

Arkad raised a finger and observed that every want disguises itself as a need at the moment when one feels it most keenly. His remedy was simple and rather old-fashioned: when a wish seizes you, wait for one day before you act on it. A want that cannot survive a single night, he said, was never worth the silver it demanded.

From a shelf beside him Arkad took an old, scratched tablet covered in tiny marks, which he had kept during his first year of saving. He told them how startled he had been when he first read the plain lines and saw exactly where his silver had been slipping away, piece by unnoticed piece. It was a humbling discovery, he said, but also a strangely freeing one, since a leak that has been found can at last be mended.

He was careful to explain that he had never starved his needs, for a hungry or ragged man cannot work well, and work was the source of all his silver. What he had learned was merely to stop his wants from running away with everything that remained after the needs had been paid. It was not a matter of misery, he insisted, but of choosing deliberately where each piece of silver would go.

Bansir rubbed his chin and exchanged a glance with Kobbi in the golden afternoon light. “It sounds simple enough when it is said aloud,” he admitted, “but I suspect it is very hard to do.” Arkad agreed warmly and said that this was precisely why the cures were habits rather than secrets, for a secret may be learned in a moment, but a habit must be practised every day.

When a full year had passed, Arkad carried his heavy jar through the awakening streets to the house of Algamish, feeling both proud and nervous. The old money-lender looked at it for a moment without a word and then asked whether Arkad had done precisely what he had been told. It was the kind of question to which only an honest answer would do.

Arkad replied that he had followed the plan faithfully and had taken not a single piece from the jar. Algamish asked what he had done with the silver, and Arkad, whose pride suddenly deserted him, had to confess that it sat on a shelf in his room. He felt like a man who had lifted a great weight only to be asked what he had built with it.

Algamish held a silver coin up to the lamp and turned it slowly so that it glittered. He said that silver lying idle does no work for anyone, and that a wise man does not allow his savings to sleep in a jar but lends them carefully so that they may earn. A coin that is hidden, he added, is a servant who has been locked in a cupboard.

Arkad pointed out, with some anxiety, that he did not know whom he could trust with his hard-won savings. Algamish gave him a single rule, which was to lend only to men who had a clear use for the silver and a clear way of paying it back. He was not to lend to a man who merely hoped, or merely promised, or merely smiled.

Not long afterwards Arkad met a brickmaker who stood beside a great stack of unbaked bricks, looking at his cold and empty kiln. The man needed silver to buy clay and wood for the fire so that he could fill a large order, and he had no other way of finding it. Arkad saw at once that here was a use for silver that was real, visible and honest.

Arkad and the brickmaker agreed upon a day for repayment and upon a fair sum to be paid on top, and they marked the terms on a clay tablet that each of them kept. Arkad lent only a part of his savings, for Algamish had warned him never to place everything in a single spot. He walked away feeling both excited and strangely exposed, as though he had set a part of himself on the road.

In the weeks that followed, Arkad lay awake more than once, staring at the dark roof and listening to the city sleep. He kept asking himself whether he would ever see that silver again, and whether the pleasant old money-lender had led him into folly. Every sound at the door made his heart jump, and every day dragged by like a month.

On the promised day the brickmaker came striding toward Arkad beside the glowing kiln, smelling of smoke and clay, and placed a heavy bag in his hands. Inside lay every piece of silver that Arkad had lent, together with the fair payment that they had agreed upon, counted out without a shortfall. The man even thanked him, as though he were the one who had received a gift.

Arkad counted the silver twice and then a third time, scarcely believing what he saw. Silver that he had not laboured for, silver that had grown quietly while he slept, now lay in a neat pile on his table, and it was proof that Algamish had been right. Within the hour he had decided to lend again, more carefully than before, and to write every detail of the loan upon a tablet of his own.

Arkad raised three fingers and named the third cure for a lean purse, which was to make one's gold multiply by putting every piece to work. Kobbi frowned, for the idea seemed to him a dangerous one, and he asked what would become of a man who lent his gold and never saw it again. Arkad nodded gravely, as if he had been waiting for that very question all afternoon.

Arkad shook his head slowly and looked at the quiet water of the pool, as though he could see his younger self reflected in it. “I was proud of my small success,” he said, “and pride is a poor adviser for a man with money.” Before long, a friend had come to him with an exciting plan to trade in jewels.

The friend spoke swiftly and with shining eyes beside a bright stall in the market, waving his hands as though the jewels were already spread before them. He said that fine stones could be bought for almost nothing in a far country and sold at enormous profit at home, and that a man had only to be brave enough to try. Arkad, who had never been offered a great opportunity before, found himself nodding along.

Neither of them knew the first thing about stones, but the plan sounded so wonderful that Arkad forgot every doubt he had ever held. He lent his friend a large part of his savings, counting it out with a trembling hand, and sent him on his way with the warmest of good wishes. It did not once occur to him to ask anybody who understood the jewel trade what they thought of the scheme.

Many months later, the friend came walking back through the city gate, weary and dusty and plainly unhappy, and he carried a small bag in his hand. He could not look Arkad in the eye as he explained what had happened, and his voice shook as though he expected to be struck. The bag held only a handful of coloured stones, and not one of them looked as splendid as the stones in his promises.

A grey-haired dealer in stones held up the largest piece to the light, turned it slowly and then shook his head with the weary patience of an expert. The pieces were worth almost nothing, he told them gently, and anyone who knew the trade would have seen it at a single glance. His words fell like pebbles into a deep well, and Arkad listened to the silence that followed.

The silver was gone, and Arkad sat alone that night with his empty purse and a bag of worthless stones, wondering how a man could have been so foolish. His friend had been honest enough, but honesty had not saved the money, for ignorance had spent it as surely as any thief could have done. Shame kept Arkad silent, and for several days he told no one what had happened.

For days Arkad avoided the house of Algamish, but in the end he went there with his head bowed, as a boy goes to confess a broken window. He told the old man the whole story from beginning to end, and he did not try to leave out the parts that made him look foolish. It was, he later said, the hardest speech he had ever made, and the one that he was most glad to have delivered.

Algamish listened without a word, poured two cups of water and set one in front of Arkad, as if nothing important had happened. He did not scold or sneer, but he said, kindly enough, that Arkad had now paid for a lesson, and that many men pay far more for the same one. A loss that teaches, he added, is a better teacher than a gain that does not.

From that day onward, Arkad made a habit of going to those who understood each trade before he lent a single piece of silver. He sat in the market square and listened to wise men, and he learned that there is no shame in asking questions, only in failing to ask them. Gradually the habit became second nature, and he found that a few honest questions could save him a great deal of grief.

In the garden, Bansir nodded slowly, and Arkad lifted four fingers into the afternoon light. “The fourth cure,” he said, “is to guard your gold against loss, by lending only where the risk is small and the advice of the wise is good.” He spoke the words quietly, but they carried the weight of a lesson that had been paid for in silver.

Arkad pointed up at the roof and the strong, plain walls of the house around them, and he smiled as though greeting a faithful old friend. “The fifth cure for a lean purse,” he said, “is to make a home of your own into a good investment.” The two visitors looked up and saw for the first time how solid and unremarkable the house really was.

For many years Arkad had lived in rented rooms, and each season he had counted out a fixed sum for a landlord whose face he scarcely knew. At the end of every year he had owned nothing, while the landlord had owned everything, and the arrangement had seemed to Arkad perfectly natural. It was not until Algamish mentioned the matter that he had begun to see it clearly.

Algamish had told him, in his dry and exact manner, that a man who owns his own home keeps his silver in his own family. A tenant, he said, pays handsomely every year for a roof that will never become his, and the money disappears into another man's coffers without leaving so much as a brick behind. A wise man prefers to pay for something that will remain standing long after he is gone.

So Arkad bought a small house with part of his savings and paid off the remainder in small, regular parts over the following years, as a man might climb a long flight of steps. It was not a grand house, but it had a brick courtyard, a sound roof and a door that nobody else could ever lock against him. The day he held the final tablet, marked as paid, he sat in the doorway and said nothing for a long time.

In the evenings, Arkad's family gathered in the courtyard, and the house was filled with warmth, the smell of supper and the quiet laughter of people who feel safe. Nobody there feared the knock of a landlord at the door, and none of them thought of the walls as anything but their own. Arkad felt, as he watched them, that few pieces of silver in his whole life had been better spent.

Bansir looked around at his own thoughts and found himself picturing the rented workshop at home, with its old chariot frame and its crooked door that never quite closed. Every month he paid a sum of silver to the man who owned the place, and in all those years he had never once asked himself what he would have to show for it. The question settled upon his shoulders with a weight that he had not expected, and he did not know how to answer it.

Arkad turned and gestured toward an old porter who rested in the shade of a distant wall, his basket on the ground beside him. “The sixth cure,” he said gently, “is to plan an income for your old age and for the protection of your family.” The words seemed to hang in the warm afternoon air as the three men watched the old man breathe.

The porter had carried heavy loads for merchants since boyhood, and nobody in Babylon had ever called him lazy. Now his back was bent, his hands were knotted and his basket had grown too heavy for him, so that he rested more often than he worked. Arkad pointed him out with sorrow rather than scorn, for the old man's story could have been the story of almost anyone.

Arkad spoke quietly, because he did not wish the old man to overhear, and he told his guests that silver must be set to work while a man is still strong. In that way, he said, it will be earning faithfully on the day when his own strength has gone, or when his family is in need and he is not there to provide. A wise man builds his shelter in the summer, long before the first rain.

Kobbi rubbed his fingers slowly and gazed down at his lute, and a shadow crossed his face. He had never once thought about the day when his hands would grow stiff and the music would stop, and the thought made his chest feel suddenly cold. Neither he nor Bansir spoke, and the three of them sat together in thoughtful silence while the fountain murmured on.

Arkad raised seven fingers and smiled at the two friends, who had been listening with growing attention. “The seventh cure,” he said, “is to increase your own ability to earn, for the best purse in the world is a pair of skilled and willing hands.” He spoke the words like a man handing over a final and much-treasured key.

Arkad turned to Bansir and asked quietly whether he knew his craft as well as any man in Babylon. Bansir opened his mouth to answer proudly, but he found, to his own surprise, that he could not say yes with an honest heart. He had built chariots for twenty years, and yet he suspected that he had learned very little in the last ten.

A man who wishes to learn will grow, Arkad said, and a man who stops learning will always remain small, however hard he labours. He added that people who understand their work thoroughly are paid for their knowledge as well as for their effort, and that knowledge is the one possession no thief can carry off. The hours spent in learning, he told them, are the most profitable hours a worker ever spends.

When Arkad was a young scribe, he had set himself to copy faster and with fewer mistakes, and he had practised each evening until his fingers ached. Within a year the other men in the lane had begun to remark that Arkad's tablets were the cleanest and quickest in the city. Neither he nor they could say exactly when the change had come, for improvement arrives quietly, like dawn.

He had also learned to read and understand the laws and trading records that he copied, instead of merely pressing them into clay without a thought. Algamish noticed the change almost at once, and he began to pay Arkad more than he paid any of the other scribes, because a scribe who understands is worth far more than one who only obeys. It was the first time that Arkad had been rewarded for something other than his time.

Kobbi stared up at the sky and moved his fingers as though he held a lute, and a new thought stirred behind his tired eyes. He had never learned the songs of other lands, nor tried to teach his art to anyone, and he wondered whether eager young players might pay to learn from him. The idea was so new to him that he turned it over cautiously, like a coin from a foreign country.

Bansir drew a wheel in the dust with a stick, studied it for a moment, and then sketched a second wheel beside it, lighter and more finely shaped. He pictured a stronger axle, a quicker way of fitting the bronze, and an apprentice who might share the work and learn the craft in turn. It struck him that he had never once asked himself how his skill could be made to grow.

A servant brought bread, figs and cool water on a tray and set it on a low table in the shade, and the three men ate slowly while the shadows lengthened. They talked easily now, and each of them found himself describing what he might learn and make if he set his mind to it. The simple meal tasted better than any feast that Kobbi had ever played at.

Arkad broke a flat loaf in half and passed one piece to each guest, and then he reminded them with a smile that none of the seven cures works in a day. Each cure, he said, works a little every day if it is kept faithfully, in the same way that a drop of water, given years, will wear a groove into stone. It was patience, rather than any special cleverness, that had made him rich, and he never pretended otherwise.

Bansir looked at the pale clay tablet that lay in front of him and asked whether there was anything more that he ought to understand. “There is,” said Arkad, rising to his feet and brushing the crumbs from his robe. “The cures tell a man what he should do, but there are also five laws of gold that explain why those cures work.”

Arkad went into the house and returned after a moment with a heavy clay tablet, which he laid carefully on the courtyard table between the cups. Long ago, he said, he had written five laws of gold for his own son, who was setting out to find his fortune in the world. Each law had been scratched into the clay as a father scratches wisdom into a child's memory, with love and a little fear.

Arkad lifted one finger and let the quiet settle over the courtyard before he spoke. “The first law,” he said, “is that gold comes gladly and in growing quantity to the man who keeps at least a tenth of all that he earns.” It sounded so simple that Kobbi almost laughed, and then he remembered how long it had taken him to begin.

A tenth of even a poor man's pay, Arkad told them, becomes a heavy jar in time, and a heavy jar becomes a lending, and a lending becomes a fortune. The jar does not grow because its owner is clever or lucky, but because he keeps adding to it, week after week, without pausing to ask whether the weeks are worth the trouble. A habit, once begun, is the quietest and most reliable of servants, and it asks for nothing but to be repeated.

Arkad weighed a small bag of silver in the palm of his hand and smiled as he felt its modest weight. “The second law,” he said, “is that gold works hard and contentedly for the wise owner who finds good and profitable work for it to do.” Left alone, he explained, it multiplies as quietly as a flock in a green field.

Arkad reminded them that his silver had earned more silver while he slept, while he ate, and while he walked through the crowded market, never complaining and never asking for a reward. Gold, unlike the people who own it, does not tire, does not grumble and does not need a day of rest. A wise man, he said, therefore makes sure that it is always busy, and never left to sleep in a jar.

Kobbi and Bansir leaned closer as Arkad's finger travelled down to the next line of the tablet, and the shadows of the palm trees crept a little farther across the stones. “The third law,” he said, “is that gold stays with the careful owner who asks the advice of the wise.” He paused, and added with a faint smile that the wise are not always the ones who speak the loudest in the market.

Arkad said that the advice of the wise had cost him only a question or two, and that those few questions had saved him many pieces of silver over the years. In all his dealings, he said, no bargain had been cheaper than a few minutes of honest listening. A man who is too proud to ask, he warned, is simply a man who has decided to learn the lesson the expensive way.

Arkad lifted a glittering stone from a small bowl, held it up to the light for a moment, and shook his head with a rueful smile. “The fourth law,” he said, “is that gold slips away from the man who puts it into things he does not understand, or that are not approved by those who do.” It was a law that he had written out of his own pain, and he did not need to look at the tablet to recite it.

As the afternoon faded, servants came softly into the courtyard and lit the oil lamps one after another until the whole place glowed. “The fifth and last law,” said Arkad, “is that gold flees from those who demand impossible gains, or who follow the advice of tricksters and schemers.” His tone was gentle, but nobody present doubted that he meant every word, or that he had learned each one dearly.

Arkad laid the tablet down very gently, as if it were a sleeping child. The five laws were as short as a breath, he said, but a man needs a whole lifetime to learn to keep them, and he must begin again each morning. Kobbi leaned forward, for there was one question that the laws had not answered, and it concerned the strange and unreliable gift called luck.

Kobbi leaned forward with a puzzled look while Arkad poured cool water for his guests, for there was one thing that still troubled him, and he asked about luck. It seemed to him that certain fortunate men found silver in the road without the smallest effort or merit. If gold came so easily to some, he wondered, then why should the rest of them trouble to keep jars at all?

Arkad smiled, as though he had been waiting for the question, and said that he would tell them the tale of Hadan the potter. Hadan lived in a lane beside the river, where the clay was good and the smoke from the kilns hung blue over the water, and he made handsome jars that people were glad to buy. For all that, he had never in his life been able to keep a piece of silver for more than a few days.

One morning Hadan was pulling his cart of jars along the road toward the market when he saw something lying in the dust beside a boundary stone. It was a heavy purse, and when he opened it with shaking fingers, he found more silver than he could have earned in a whole year of honest work. For a moment he forgot to breathe, and the donkey beside him might have been a statue.

Hadan looked up and down the road, but not a soul was in sight, and he did the honest thing and asked every traveller he met whether a purse had been lost. Some shook their heads, some shrugged, and a few looked at the purse with a hunger that made him close his hand over it. In the end nobody came forward to claim it, and the silver was his.

At last Hadan decided that fortune had chosen him, and he set about making up for all the lean years at once. He bought a fine robe with a border of blue thread, gave a great feast to which half the lane was invited, and purchased a handsome donkey that he did not need. For a week the lane rang with his laughter, and nobody was prouder or happier than he.

Before long he stopped making jars altogether, because he believed that a rich man had no further need of toil. His wheel stood still and his hands grew soft, and he sat beside the kiln with an empty cup and a full purse, feeling like a prince of Babylon. The days drifted by as pleasantly as clouds, and he did not notice how quickly they passed.

Season after season, the silver in the purse dwindled, while the clay in his workshop dried hard and cracked in its sacks. Hadan assured himself that he would begin again tomorrow, but tomorrow had the habit of turning into the day after, and the day after into the next season. He had given up his work for a single stroke of fortune, and fortune was a poor employer.

Meanwhile his old customers began to buy their jars from other potters in the lane, because a market does not wait for the idle. When Hadan finally wished to work again, he found that his customers had forgotten him, and that the places at the market where he had once stood were filled by strangers. His kiln was cold, his reputation had cooled with it, and his skill was out of practice.

By the end of the year the purse was empty, and Hadan was poorer than he had ever been, for now he had lost not only the silver but also his trade. He sat down at his table and counted the last few coins, and he could not understand where all that fortune had gone. The truth was that it had never been his to keep, for it had not come to him through any habit that could hold it.

Arkad lifted a hand toward his guests, and the lamplight shone briefly on his face. “Luck gave Hadan silver,” he said, “but it did not give him a habit to keep it, and a single habit would have kept the whole purse.” He added gently that luck had visited him once, and that it was not likely to knock on the same door a second time.

Arkad answered that luck gives nothing that lasts, and then he rose and fetched a small wooden chest from a corner of the courtyard. Inside, wrapped in soft cloth, lay a bundle of baked clay tablets, and he laid them out one by one in the lamplight, with the care of a man handling something very old and very fragile. His guests watched in silence, for it was clear that these were no ordinary writings.

These tablets, he said, had come from Nippur, a city far from Babylon, and they had been written by a former slave named Dabasir, in his own hand and in his own words. A traveller had brought them to him many years ago as a gift, and he had read them so often that he could nearly recite them. He would tell the story, he said, as the tablets told it, and he asked his guests to listen as if the man himself were speaking.

Dabasir had spent many years in service as a slave, carrying water, laying bricks and following the commands of others from before the sunrise until after dark. He worked hard all day and owned nothing, not even the roof over his head, and sometimes he had gone whole weeks without hearing his own name spoken kindly. It was a life that taught him to endure, but it did not teach him how to be free.

At last the day came when Dabasir was free, and he walked out into the street with his arms open, laughing at the sky as though it were a gift that had been given to him alone. For a brief and blissful time he was as happy as a boy at a festival. Then he remembered something that freedom could not wash away, and the laughter died on his lips.

He sat down in a bare room and counted his debts on a row of clay tablets, and the sums were far larger than he had dared to fear. Some of them came from the foolish days before he had been sold into service, and some he had taken on since, and altogether he owed money to the baker, the cloth-seller, the landlord and many others besides. Like many people who owe much, he was tempted to hide from the problem rather than face it.

Dabasir was so ashamed that he began to avoid the streets where his creditors lived, hurrying down narrow alleys with his head bowed and his collar turned up. At night he lay awake, hearing every footstep outside as the knock of a man who wanted his money, and by morning he felt more tired than before he had slept. His freedom, which should have been a joy, had turned into a long and anxious hiding.

After some weeks a friend, who had noticed how thin and haunted he had become, whispered to him in the market that there was a money-lender named Mathon. Mathon, said the friend, was known to be fair even to men who owed a great deal, and he had helped more than one hopeless debtor find a way out. Dabasir said that he would think about it, but he thought about little else for three days.

Dabasir found Mathon's house at last and stood in front of a broad table crowded with clay tablets, scales and small bags of silver. His mouth was dry, his knees were weak and he found that all the words he had rehearsed had fled from his head. He stood there for a long, uncomfortable moment, twisting the hem of his robe in his hands.

Mathon sat with his hands folded and waited patiently, as one waits for a shy animal to come to the hand, until Dabasir had found his voice. Then Dabasir poured out his whole story, from his years in service to the heap of debts that now seemed to crush him, and he left out no part of it. When he had finished, Mathon said quietly that most men hide from their debts, and that he did not often see one brave enough to walk through his door.

Mathon reached across the table, gave him a blank clay tablet and a reed, and set him a simple and unexpected task. Dabasir was to write down every debt he owed, with the name of every creditor and the exact sum due to each, and then to return the next day. It was the first time that anyone had asked him to look at his troubles instead of running from them.

Dabasir sat up all night beside a small lamp, writing every name and every sum on the wet clay, and when dawn came, he added the total and watched his hand begin to shake. He had known that he owed a great deal, but a feeling is one thing and a number is quite another. Yet as he looked at the plain marks, he realised that his fear had shrunk, for an enemy that has been named can at least be faced.

The next morning Mathon read the tablet slowly, with a finger moving along each line, and then he looked up with an expression that was almost kind. He said that a man who knows exactly what he owes has already begun to deal with it, and that the worst debts are those that a man is too afraid to count. The remark was brief, but Dabasir felt a small weight lift from his chest, the first in many weeks.

Mathon asked how much silver Dabasir could earn in a month if he laboured honestly and without rest. Dabasir named a modest wage, which was all that a newly freed slave could hope to find, and he waited for Mathon to laugh or shake his head. Instead the money-lender nodded gravely, as though he had been told a perfectly respectable figure.

Taking up a reed, Mathon drew a plan on a fresh tablet with quick, clean strokes, while Dabasir watched with a mixture of hope and dread. Dabasir would live on part of what he earned, said Mathon, and the remainder would be shared fairly among the people to whom he owed money, month after month, until nothing was left to pay. It was not a clever scheme, but it was an honest and practical one.

Mathon laid out small piles of silver beside a row of tablets and showed, step by step, how the sharing would work in practice. Each creditor would receive a part in proportion to the size of what he was owed, so that nobody was treated better than another and nobody was left with nothing. The simple fairness of the arrangement struck Dabasir as more comforting than any promise of sudden riches.

Then Mathon pointed to the door and told Dabasir that he must visit every creditor in person, for a debt that is discussed by messenger is easily misunderstood. He should show each one the tablet and explain the plan honestly, face to face, without excuses and without flattery. It was the hardest part of the plan, and Mathon did not pretend otherwise.

At the baker's door, Dabasir's heart pounded so hard that he could feel it in his throat, and he held his tablet in both hands like a shield. The baker listened to the whole plan with floury arms folded and a thoughtful frown, and at the end he said that he would far rather receive a little each month than nothing at all. Dabasir walked away from the shop feeling that the street itself had grown wider and lighter.

The cloth-seller folded his arms and grumbled loudly about the time he had already waited, but in the end he agreed to the plan. Another creditor was angry and raised his voice until the neighbours stared, yet Dabasir stayed calm and simply showed him the tablet once more, line by line. He had learned in his years of service that patience can outlast a great deal of anger.

When Dabasir returned, Mathon set a heavy clay weight on one side of a balance scale and watched the empty pan on the other side rise. A man should borrow only what he can repay, he said, and he should think carefully about the weight of a loan before he picks it up. A debt, he added, has a way of becoming heavier with every day that it is ignored.

Mathon rested his hand on the scale and explained that loans for pleasure are always the heaviest, because they leave nothing behind to carry the weight. Then he sent Dabasir out into the evening with a plan, a tablet and a little more courage than he had known for years. The streets that had frightened him now seemed simply streets, filled with people who had also, perhaps, been afraid.

Dabasir found work with a trader who needed a strong man to load goods onto camels at the edge of the city, and he took it gladly. The wages were small, but they were his own, and for the first time in many years he felt that he was moving in the right direction. Each morning he rose before the sun and was grateful for the very weight of the sacks.

Each month, before he spent a single piece of silver on himself, Dabasir set aside the portion that belonged to his creditors. He did not wait to see what was left over, because he knew from long experience that nothing is ever left over for the man who pays himself first and the world last. The habit was strict, but it brought a quiet and unfamiliar kind of peace.

There were lean times, and in one of them a friend invited him to a lively feast with music, roasted meat and cups of honeyed wine. Dabasir thanked him warmly and refused, and he went home through the dark streets to his bread and his tablet, feeling lonely but not defeated. A man cannot win a hard battle and a pleasant evening in the same night, he told himself, and he chose the battle.

One creditor lost his patience and demanded all of his silver at once, thumping the table so that the cups jumped. Dabasir held up the tablet calmly, showed the plan and the marks that proved his payments, and Mathon himself came to speak on his behalf. The word of an honest lender, it seemed, carried more weight than a loud voice, and the angry man at last fell silent.

Slowly, as the seasons passed, the debts began to grow smaller, and the marks on the tablets showed the change in neat and encouraging lines. The baker, with a broad and floury smile, drew a line through the first debt and wrote the word paid, and Dabasir felt a joy that he had not known since the day of his freedom. It was a small victory, but small victories are the stones of which long roads are built.

In the second year, Dabasir fell ill and could not work for a whole month, and he lay in his bare room listening to the sounds of the street. He did not hide from his creditors, as the old Dabasir would have done, but sent word to each of them and told them honestly what had happened. It was hard to confess his weakness, but harder still, he knew, to let them wonder.

The creditors agreed to wait, because Dabasir had always dealt with them fairly and had never broken a promise or missed a payment without warning. When at last he recovered, he worked harder than before, and the share that he set aside was never again late, even by a single day. His reputation, once a burden, had become a kind of silver that he could not spend but could not lose.

At last the day came when Dabasir walked to the baker's shop with the final piece of silver in his hand, though it felt heavier than any he had ever carried. The baker took it, laughed aloud, and clasped his hand across the counter as though they had been friends for many years. There was flour on both their hands, and neither of them cared, for it was the happiest handshake of the baker's year.

That night Dabasir owed nothing to anyone in the world, and he slept more soundly than he had slept since boyhood, with the morning sun falling across his face. When he woke, he walked down the street with his head held high and looked every man in the eye, and he found that the city seemed larger and kinder than before. For the first time he understood what freedom had been waiting to give him.

The last of the tablets said that a man who pays his debts is truly free, and that he should then begin to keep a tenth of all that he earns. Kobbi, listening quietly, thought of the baker to whom he owed a few coins, and the cake-seller to whom he owed a few more, and found that his face had grown warm. He resolved, there and then, to write down their names on a tablet of his own, beginning that very night.

Bansir leaned forward in the lamplight and asked whether Arkad had lent only to the brickmaker, or whether others, too, had come knocking at his door. Arkad laughed softly and said that there had been many, for as his savings grew, so did the number of people who had suddenly discovered how much they needed silver. Some of them were honest, some were merely hopeful, and a few were neither, which is why he learned to ask before he answered.

One year, two camel traders in dusty cloaks came to his door with a clay tablet in their hands and the weariness of a long journey in their faces. They needed silver to buy camels for a new caravan, they said, and they promised to repay him, with a fair sum on top, when they returned from the desert. Arkad thanked them for their honesty and asked them to wait a few days while he made inquiries of his own.

Arkad did not say yes at once, for he had not forgotten his lesson with the jewels. Instead he went to a grey-bearded caravan master, a man whose face had been carved by sun and sand, and asked him many questions about camels, roads and the profits of the trade. The old man answered each one patiently, as a teacher answers a promising pupil.

Arkad wanted to know how many camels the traders needed, which road they planned to take, what they intended to carry and how long they would be away. He wrote down every answer on a clay tablet, so that he could weigh them against one another later in the quiet of his own room. A decision made on the strength of a smile, he reflected, is a decision made on very little.

Arkad lent only to men who knew their trade thoroughly, and he asked for a clear promise written on a tablet that both parties kept. He shook hands with the two traders over the signed clay, and they thanked him with a respect that he found both pleasing and slightly alarming. It is a serious thing, he thought, to be trusted with another man's livelihood.

The caravan left through the city gate at sunset, a long line of camels swaying against a sky of red and gold, and the bells rang softly in the dust. Arkad stood among the onlookers and watched until the last animal had vanished into the fading light, and then he walked home with the strange hollow feeling of a man who has sent a piece of himself into the wilderness. There was nothing to do now but wait, and waiting, he was to discover, is a harder labour than carrying sacks.

During the weeks of waiting, a rumour of a great sandstorm reached the city, and Arkad stood on his roof at night, gazing at the empty road that led into the darkness. He was anxious and slept little, but he took some comfort in knowing that he had not lent the whole of his silver to a single caravan. He remembered the old warning of Algamish, and for once he was grateful for a lesson that had been so costly.

At last, early one morning, the first caravan came back through the gate with its bells ringing and its camels heavy with cloth and spice. The traders were weary and sunburned but beaming, and they repaid Arkad in full, with a fair payment on top, counting out the silver on the very spot where he had first lent it. Arkad could scarcely keep from smiling like a boy, for the first time his judgement had been repaid by the road itself.

A second caravan arrived many days later, with half-empty baskets and camels so tired that they could barely lift their heads. It had lost part of its goods on the road and could repay Arkad only slowly, in small parts, but because he had spread his silver among several ventures, the loss did not wound him. He waited patiently, accepted what was offered and wrote each payment on the tablet.

Arkad poured water for his guests and observed that gold lent in many places, to people who thoroughly know their trade, is guarded by that very spread. “One caravan may fail,” he said, “but a wise lender does not allow a single caravan to decide the fate of his whole fortune.” He sipped his water and added that he had been told this long before he understood it.

Another year, a sheep farmer in a woolly hat came to Arkad's gate with his cap crushed in his hands and the smell of fields still on his clothes. He asked for silver to buy more ewes, and he spoke simply and without ornament, like a man who is used to the open air and the honest weather. Arkad liked him at once, but he kept his liking to himself until he had asked a few questions of his own.

The farmer drew his plan in the dust with the end of his crook, tracing the year as though it were a road. Lambs would be born in the spring, he said, wool would be sheared in the summer, and he would repay Arkad when the wool was sold at the market in the autumn. It was a clear plan, and every part of it depended on the seasons rather than on luck.

Arkad went out to see the farm for himself, and he found a flock spread over green fields beside the river, white against the grass like scattered clouds. He was glad to see that the farmer knew each animal and spoke to it by name, for a man who knows his flock is not likely to waste it. The river murmured, the sheep grazed, and Arkad's doubts melted away like morning mist in the warm sun.

At dawn the farmer held a newborn lamb in his arms, still damp and trembling, and told Arkad that no lamb comes in a day. A flock must be fed and watched and sheltered, he said, and a man must be willing to wait for its seasons, because wanting something quickly does not hurry the sun. Arkad listened, and the words stayed with him long after he had gone home.

That summer was dry, and the grass grew thin and brown beneath a merciless sun, and the farmer walked among his ewes with a worried frown. Arkad did not call for his silver early, however, for he had agreed to wait and a man who breaks his word in a drought has little right to expect kindness in a flood. The days dragged on, and the sky stayed empty of rain, but the flock held together and so did the farmer's courage.

In the autumn the rains came at last, the sheep were sheared in the shaded yard, and the heaped wool was sold at the market for a good price. The farmer came to Arkad with a heavy bag and repaid him in full, with a fair payment on top, and for a moment neither of them could think of anything to say. Then they both laughed at last, like men who have survived a storm and are surprised to find the sun still shining.

The farmer had not sold his ewes for quick silver, though he had been sorely tempted in the dry months, and that restraint had saved him. Arkad saw that gold grows like a flock when it is kept and fed, and that it fails when it is eaten too soon, for a flock that is eaten cannot bear lambs. It was a lesson that he would repeat to himself for the rest of his life.

In the second year the flock was larger, and the farmer repaid Arkad more than before and with an easier smile. Before long he owned the very field where his sheep had grazed, and he built himself a bigger barn with a sound roof, proud as a king in his new palace. The patient labour of two seasons had changed the whole shape of his life.

Arkad rested a hand on the garden wall as the evening settled around them, and his voice was gentle. Many men want a harvest in a week, he told Bansir, and so they never plant anything at all, because the fields demand a season and the men demand a day. He said that the real work of gold is done in the dark, like the roots of a tree.

Kobbi sighed and leaned back against a pillar of the courtyard, and he said that patience was a very hard trade indeed. “You may say so,” Arkad replied with a smile, “but it is learned like any other, one small day at a time, and the best teacher is a jar that grows heavier each week.” Kobbi laughed in spite of himself, and for the first time that day he did not feel the weight of the long road ahead.

Years went by, and Arkad's savings had grown so large that the whole city knew his name and many people claimed to have known him in his youth. More and more of them came to his door, and a great number brought plans, requests and tablets crowded with promises, each one more urgent than the last. He learned to listen to all of them politely and to believe almost none of them at first.

One morning a stranger in a bright robe arrived at the gate with a leather bag in his hand and a smile that was a little too wide. He greeted the servant so warmly, and with so many compliments to the household, that the man almost let him in without asking his name. Arkad, watching from an upper window, felt a small, cool doubt settle in his mind.

The stranger bowed low in the doorway and called Arkad the wisest and most respected man in all Babylon, and his words flowed like oil from a jar. Every sentence seemed to have been polished for the occasion, and every one of them was designed to please. Arkad noticed that the stranger spoke a great deal about Arkad and very little about anything else.

Leaning close, he whispered that he knew of a secret trade that could double Arkad's silver in a single month, with no risk and no trouble at all. He would take only a small share for himself, he assured Arkad, and Arkad could not possibly lose, since the plan was so clever that it could not fail. He seemed to find this explanation entirely satisfying, and he waited for Arkad to reach for his purse.

Arkad asked a few plain questions, as he had been taught to do, wanting to know which trade it was, along which road it travelled and who else had already joined. The stranger spread his hands wide and smiled and answered with long, flowing speeches that somehow managed to say nothing at all. After a long while, Arkad knew exactly as much as he had known at the start.

Arkad said courteously that he would think the matter over, and he sent a servant to fetch two grey-bearded wise men whose judgement he trusted. They came at once and sat down in the courtyard with a clay tablet between them, their faces grave and their eyes alert. The stranger shifted a little in his chair, and for the first time his smile lost some of its shine.

The wise men studied the stranger's proposal for a long time, passing the tablet from hand to hand and murmuring to each other in low voices. At last they shook their heads, and the older one said that no honest trade doubles silver in a single month without great danger to those who lend. If such a thing were easy, he added, the stranger would hardly be wandering from door to door looking for lenders.

Arkad refused, politely but firmly, and he thanked the stranger for coming as though nothing unpleasant had happened. The stranger's smile faded like a lamp running out of oil, and he hurried away from the gate with his bag clutched tightly under his arm and his bright robe flapping behind him. Arkad watched him go and felt neither anger nor triumph, only a sort of tired relief.

Some months later, news ran through the city that the stranger had taken silver from many people in the lower streets, promising them what he had promised Arkad. When they came to look for him, they found only an empty house, a cold hearth and a few broken promises, and the silver was never seen again. Several of those people, Arkad later learned, had been saving for years and had trusted the stranger with every piece.

Arkad lifted the old tablet and looked gravely at Bansir in the lamplight, and the flame wavered between them. “When a plan sounds too good to be true,” he said, “it is wise to ask who really gains from it, and why a stranger should wish to share his good fortune with you.” Bansir, who had been sitting very still while the lamplight moved across his face, nodded slowly and said nothing.

As the evening deepened, Arkad led his guests across the garden to the far wall, past the pool, which had turned from silver to deep blue. From there they could see the great wall of Babylon standing above the rooftops, its bricks glowing faintly in the last light of the sun. For a moment nobody spoke, and the same wall that had sheltered the friends the evening before now seemed to look down on them with a different expression.

Arkad said that savings are like a city wall, for they stand between a family and the wolves of bad luck, and a man does not notice them on a calm day. He is glad of them, however, on a stormy night, when sickness comes or the harvest fails or a good customer does not pay. It is only when the wind rises, he added, that a man learns whether the wall he built was thick enough.

The great wall had taken many hands and many years to build, Arkad reminded them, and not one of the men who laid its first bricks had lived to see it finished. A purse is made in much the same way, he said, one brick at a time, and no single brick looks important by itself. What matters is the patience to keep laying them, day after day, without stopping to ask when the wall will be done.

He opened his hands, palms upward, beside the lantern, and the light fell across his weathered fingers. Gold is a tool for a good life, he said, and never a prize in itself, and a man who forgets this becomes the servant of the very thing that was meant to serve him. It should buy a home, a good meal, a little music and the freedom to help others, and then it should be left to its quiet work.

Arkad told them that each year he gave a part of his silver to those who were in need, to the sick and the old and the families whose luck had failed. Kobbi was deeply moved by this, and he saw for the first time that the richest man in Babylon valued his gold far less than he valued the people around him. It was, he thought, the greatest difference between this rich man and the rich merchant in the gold chariot.

At the garden gate, Arkad rested a hand on Bansir's shoulder and looked at him with great seriousness. “These habits must be kept for years,” he said, “and not for a single day, however bright and strong the resolve of that day may seem.” Bansir felt the warmth of the hand through his thin robe and understood that the old man spoke from long experience.

Bansir looked at his empty hands under the stars and asked, in a low voice, how they would know that the plan was working. He was not doubting Arkad, but he was afraid of being disappointed again, as he had been disappointed so many times before in his hopes of becoming rich. Arkad, who understood the fear, did not smile at the question, but answered it as gravely as it had been asked.

Arkad lifted his old jar and held it gently, as though it were a living thing, and he told them that at first they would see nothing at all. For weeks the jar would be light and the effort would feel foolish, he said, but one day it would be too heavy to lift with a single hand, and then they would know. Until that day, they must trust the slow arithmetic of habit, which never hurries and never lies.

The friends thanked Arkad with all their hearts and bowed at the gate, and each of them felt that he had been given something much greater than advice. Arkad told them that they should come back in a year and show him their jars, and that he would be glad to see them, whatever the jars contained. A year, he added, is not long for a man who has decided to change his life.

Bansir and Kobbi walked home together through the quiet streets, under a sky crowded with bright stars, past shuttered shops and sleeping dogs. They did not talk much, because both of them were turning over everything that they had heard, and the words that Arkad had spoken seemed to follow them along the road. The city that had seemed so cold the evening before now seemed full of quiet possibilities.

At the crossroads, beneath a hanging lantern that swayed in the night breeze, the two friends stood still for a moment and looked at each other. They agreed to begin the very next day, because they both knew that someday is a road that leads nowhere and never arrives. Neither of them wished to lie awake a third night wondering what might have been.

In the morning, Bansir bought a plain clay jar from a potter's stall in the market, paying for it without bargaining, as though it were a sacred vessel. He carried it back to his workshop and set it on a high shelf where he would see it every day but could not reach it without fetching a stool. It was the cheapest thing he had ever bought, and he suspected that it would prove the most important.

Kobbi had no new jar, but in the corner of his room he found an old one, grey with dust and cracked along one side. He wiped it clean, mended the fault with a thumb of wet clay and set it down beside his bed, where it looked rather like a small, faithful animal waiting to be fed. He wondered how long it had waited in that corner for such a purpose, and why he had never thought to give it one.

That evening Kobbi held a single silver piece over the mouth of the jar while Bansir looked on with folded arms and a face as solemn as a priest's. When the coin dropped inside it made a small, hollow sound, and the two friends looked at each other and burst out laughing like boys who have done something forbidden. It was the first piece of silver that either of them had ever kept on purpose.

At the next feast Kobbi played well, received his usual pay and counted the coins carefully when he returned home through the sleeping streets. Before he did anything else, before he bought a cake or paid a debt or so much as hung up his lute, he set aside a tenth of them and dropped them into the jar. The habit, he found, was easier to begin on a night when the music was still ringing in his ears.

In the first months Kobbi often passed a market stall piled with bright cloaks, his purse in his hand and his good resolutions in his heart, and one cloak in particular pulled at him. It was the colour of the evening sky over the river, with a border of gold thread, and he stood in front of it for a long time while the seller watched him with hope. The want was so strong that it almost felt like a need, which was exactly what Arkad had warned him about.

At last he thought of the jar and of Arkad's old advice about waiting one day, and he turned away from the stall with his purse still unopened. By the time he reached the city wall the wish had faded, and he was almost surprised to find that it had gone, like a small cloud that has crossed a very large sky. He told himself that he would look at the cloak again tomorrow, and by tomorrow he had forgotten it.

Each evening the two friends met at the wall, where they had first spoken of Arkad, and asked one another whether they had set aside their tenth. It was a small question, but it was a great deal easier to keep a promise when somebody else was waiting to hear about it, and neither man wished to be the first to confess a failure. They began to look forward to the question more than to the answer, and the wall became their small council chamber.

Some of their neighbours laughed at them and called them hoarders, and a few said that they were wasting their lives, stuffing silver into jars instead of enjoying the sweetness of the day. Bansir and Kobbi only smiled, for each week the jars were growing heavier and the laughter was growing lighter, and they had no wish to argue with men who had never tried. They had learned that a habit does not need an audience to succeed, only a morning on which it is repeated.

After one full year, the friends carried their jars through the waking city and the quiet quarter to Arkad's garden, walking carefully as though each jar were full of eggs. Arkad lifted the first one, felt its weight in his hands and smiled warmly, as though he had been waiting for them all that time. Then he took the second, weighed it too and nodded slowly, and the two friends felt something in their chests that was almost like pride.

Arkad set the two jars side by side on a stone table and smiled at them as though they were old friends who had finally learned to behave. Now, he said, their silver must learn to work, and they should lend a little of it to someone who knew his trade well. He reminded them that they must ask first, and listen to the answer, and keep their jars from becoming too proud.

Bansir first went to a wise old carpenter and asked what he thought, and the old man said that the young man in question was honest, skilled and slow to boast. Then Bansir lent a small sum so that the young man could buy new tools, and he marked the terms on a tablet in a careful hand. He felt, for the first time, a quiet satisfaction at being a man who helped another to work.

Kobbi lent a small sum to a maker of reed pipes whose work he had known for many years and whose notes he trusted completely. He had played the man's pipes at a hundred feasts, and he could hear for himself that they were good, so that he lent without any of the old fear. It struck him that a musician's ear, rightly used, was also a kind of business sense.

Both loans were repaid on the day that had been agreed, each with a fair payment on top, and the two friends counted the silver together beside the city wall. They looked at each other and smiled, because for the first time in their lives they had seen their own savings at work, patient and faithful as Arkad had promised. It felt almost like watching a small green plant push up through the dry ground after a long winter.

After some years, their purses were fatter and their lives were calmer, and the old anxious sense of being chased had gone from their faces. Bansir moved into a larger workshop where an apprentice learned at his side, and he taught the boy as carefully as he had once been taught himself, with patience and a high standard. He found that he enjoyed the work more than before, and that his chariots were better.

One spring morning Bansir placed his silver on a landlord's table and received in return a clay tablet marked paid, which made the workshop wholly his own. He walked home slowly through the market, touching the doorframe of his shop as though it might disappear if he were not careful, and a foolish smile spread across his face. It was the same door that he had always known, but it was no longer the same door.

Kobbi played at feasts without the old anxious hurry for the coins, and he found that his music was better for it, warmer and more patient. On quiet afternoons he also taught young players in a sunny courtyard, and the children of the lane learned to love the lute, and some of them grew up to play it well. He had never imagined that he would be known for anything but his own songs.

When Arkad had grown older, the friends visited him again in the quiet garden, with its pool and its palms, and they told him all that had happened since the day of the jars. He listened with great pleasure, nodding at each part as a gardener nods at a tree that has taken root, and he said that now they were ready to teach. It was the highest praise that he knew how to give, and the friends did not forget it.

Many years later, the two old friends sat by the great wall at sunset, as they did on most evenings, with their backs against the warm bricks and the noise of the city fading around them. A young man with a tired face and dusty sandals sat down a little distance away, saying nothing, and for a long time the three of them watched the light go. The sun painted the wall the colour of honey, as it had on the evening when two empty purses first sat there.

The young man turned his empty purse over, shook out a little dust and asked why hard work always left it so light, and the two old friends looked at each other and smiled. They told him that there was no secret, only a habit that begins on any ordinary day, and that the best day to begin was the one that he happened to be standing in. Then, as the first stars appeared above the wall and the lamps of Babylon began to glow, they showed him how.
